index_text:
Regulation / Governance
The Colorado River Compact of 1922 apportioned 7.5 million acre-feet annually to each of the Upper and Lower Basins for beneficial consumptive use, with the Lower Basin given the right to increase its use by an additional 1 MAF annually.
This 1922 apportionment is the foundational legal allocation that every later Lake Powell/Lake Mead operating rule, shortage tier, and interim guideline is built on top of.
source_locators: extracted text; Colorado River Compact

index_text:
Operation Rules
Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines, Reclamation triggers the first level of Lake Mead shortage (Tier One Shortage Condition) when Lake Mead's storage pool elevation falls below 1,075 feet, at which point Arizona and Nevada water deliveries are curtailed below contracted levels.
This elevation trigger is the operative rule that converts a specific Lake Mead pool elevation directly into mandatory Lower Basin delivery curtailments.
source_locators: extracted text; Annual Operations

index_text:
Operation Rules
The 2019 Drought Contingency Plans overlaid a new Tier Zero shortage condition on the 2007 Interim Guidelines, triggered at higher Lake Mead elevations of up to 1,090 feet.
Tier Zero moved the first shortage response point higher up the elevation curve, triggering conservation action earlier than the original 2007 guidelines allowed.
source_locators: extracted text; Annual Operations

index_text:
Emergency Operations
Under the Upper Basin Drought Contingency Plan's Drought Response Operations Agreement (DROA), Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool.
3,525 feet functions as an early-warning buffer elevation that triggers emergency upstream reservoir releases well before Lake Powell reaches the 3,490-foot hydropower cutoff.
source_locators: extracted text; Upper Basin Drought Contingency Plan

index_text:
Operation Failure
Absent major interventions—660,000 AF to 1 MAF of additional releases from Flaming Gorge Reservoir and 1.48 MAF of reduced Lower Basin releases from Glen Canyon Dam—Reclamation projected Lake Powell would fall below minimum power pool (3,490 feet) by August 2026.
This 2026 near-term projection shows the system operating right at the edge of hydropower failure, with the reduced Lower Basin releases also risking the basin's first-ever compact call.
source_locators: extracted text; Recent Conditions

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
The 2007 Interim Guidelines are considered “interim” because they were scheduled to expire in 20 years, at the end of 2026, which prompted Reclamation's post-2026 operations review process.
The 2026 expiration date is the deadline driving the entire ongoing post-2026 DEIS rulemaking process discussed throughout this report.
source_locators: extracted text; 2007 Interim Guidelines/Coordinated Operations for Lake Powell and Lake Mead

index_text:
Operation Rules
Under the Lower Basin Drought Contingency Plan, California's delivery curtailments begin at 200,000 AF per year at Lake Mead elevations of 1,040-1,045 feet, increasing by 50,000 AF for each additional 5-foot drop, to as much as 350,000 AF at elevations of 1,025 feet or lower.
This was the first-ever scheduled delivery reduction for California, a state that had previously been shielded from Lower Basin shortage curtailments.
source_locators: extracted text; Lower Basin Drought Contingency Plan

index_text:
Operation Rules
Under the 2024 near-term consensus agreement, reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases to the Lower Basin are allowed if Lake Powell elevations drop below 3,500 feet, permitting 6.0 MAF releases instead of the 7.0 MAF previously agreed under the 2007 Interim Guidelines.
This rule change let Reclamation trade lower guaranteed downstream deliveries for protecting Lake Powell storage during 2023-2026 near-term drought conditions.
source_locators: extracted text; Near-Term Operations: 2024 Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement

index_text:
Operation Rules
Reclamation's post-2026 DEIS Basic Coordination Alternative would reduce Lower Basin deliveries based on Lake Mead storage levels and water-rights priority, beginning at Lake Mead elevation 1,160 feet and increasing linearly to a maximum of 1.48 MAF per year at 1,110 feet or lower.
This is the least-restrictive of the four proposed post-2026 alternatives, giving a baseline against which the DEIS's more aggressive shortage-sharing options can be compared.
source_locators: extracted text; Lower Basin Shortage Guidelines

index_text:
Operation Rules
The DEIS Basic Coordination Alternative's coordinated reservoir operations would provide Glen Canyon Dam releases of 7.0 to 9.5 MAF depending on Lake Powell elevations, with the lowest releases occurring at or below a Lake Powell elevation of 3,525 feet.
This ties future Glen Canyon Dam release volumes directly to the same 3,525-foot buffer elevation already used as the DROA emergency trigger.
source_locators: extracted text; Coordinated Reservoir Operations/Releases from Glen Canyon Dam

index_text:
Stakeholders
Reclamation reported receiving more than 18,000 comments on the post-2026 DEIS from federal agencies, state and local governments, tribes, NGOs, academics, elected officials, and business interests.
The scale and breadth of commenters shows how many distinct interest groups have a direct stake in the post-2026 operating rules being decided.
source_locators: extracted text; Reaction to DEIS

index_text:
Operation Failure
Lower Basin states criticized the DEIS for limiting efforts to protect Glen Canyon Dam infrastructure to reduced Lake Powell releases rather than also considering structural dam modifications, calling the approach “shortsighted” and a cause of “major cuts” to Lower Basin deliveries.
This criticism frames the dam's physical release-capacity limitation, not just hydrology, as a root cause of forced Lower Basin delivery cuts under the proposed alternatives.
source_locators: extracted text; Reaction to DEIS

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
Reclamation would require congressional authorization prior to pursuing significant physical alterations to Glen Canyon Dam and related facilities to enable releases below current critical elevations.
This makes Congress, not Reclamation alone, the decision-making body for any structural fix to the dam's low-elevation release limitations.
source_locators: extracted text; Infrastructure Alterations and New Facilities

index_text:
Multiple Objectives
Comments on the post-2026 DEIS revealed considerable disagreement over which uses to prioritize—competition among irrigation, municipal and industrial water, ecosystem flows, and tribal uses—as well as how to distribute shortages and what hydrologic triggers should guide future operations.
This explicitly frames the unresolved multi-objective tradeoff (irrigation vs. M&I vs. ecosystem vs. tribal uses) that the post-2026 rulemaking must still reconcile.
source_locators: extracted text; Reaction to DEIS

index_text:
Modeling
Reclamation monitors Colorado River reservoir levels and projects them 24 months into the future in monthly “24-month studies” that model a single scenario of reservoir conditions to inform operating decisions.
The 24-month study is the recurring operational model that translates current hydrology into the near-term elevation and release projections used to trigger shortage tiers.
source_locators: extracted text; Annual Operations

index_text:
Operation Rules
Glen Canyon Dam has eight hydropower penstocks located at elevation 3,470 feet above sea level, each about 15 feet in diameter, with a combined total discharge capacity of 31,500 cubic feet per second, serving as the primary means of releasing water from the Upper to Lower Basin.
This establishes the dam's main release pathway capacity, which determines how much water can be delivered downstream under normal operations.
source_locators: extracted text; Glen Canyon Unit section

index_text:
Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
Reclamation estimates the depth for minimum power pool at Glen Canyon Dam is 20 feet above the penstocks, corresponding to elevation 3,490 feet above sea level, below which the dam cannot generate hydropower.
This is the specific engineering-based elevation threshold that defines when Glen Canyon Dam's hydropower function fails entirely.
source_locators: extracted text; Glen Canyon Unit section

index_text:
Emergency Operations
The River Outlet Works have historically only been opened when the dam was first filled, during short-term high-flow experiments, and for emergency flood releases in the early 1980s, and have never been used over extended periods.
This documents that the dam's low-level release pathway is essentially untested for sustained operation, directly relevant to any drought scenario requiring prolonged reliance on the outlets.
source_locators: extracted text; Regulation of Colorado River Flows section, footnote 18

index_text:
Emergency Operations
Under the Upper Basin Drought Response Operations Agreement (DROA), Reclamation's operational goal is to 'protect' a Lake Powell water storage elevation of 3,525 feet above sea level (35 feet above minimum power pool), primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial unit reservoirs.
This is the specific protective elevation target and mechanism basin managers use to keep Lake Powell above minimum power pool during drought.
source_locators: extracted text; Ongoing Efforts to Mitigate Long-Term Drought Effects section

index_text:
Real-Time Operations
Using DROA authorities, Reclamation transferred 180,000 acre-feet to Lake Powell in 2021 from Flaming Gorge (125,000 AF), Blue Mesa (36,000 AF), and Navajo (20,000 AF) reservoirs, and in 2022 reduced Lake Powell releases from 7.48 to 7.00 maf while transferring an additional 0.50 maf from Flaming Gorge.
These are concrete, quantified real-time drought interventions actually implemented to shore up Lake Powell storage in 2021-2022.
source_locators: extracted text; Water Year 2023 Status section (preceding paragraph)

index_text:
Observation and Data
Lake Powell's elevation on March 11, 2023, was 3,520 feet above sea level, its lowest level on record -- more than 178 feet below full storage capacity, 31 feet above minimum power pool (3,490 feet), and below Reclamation's DROA target protection elevation of 3,525 feet.
This is a concrete, dated observed record showing that even active drought interventions had not kept Lake Powell above its own protection target as of the report date.
source_locators: extracted text; Water Year 2023 Status section

index_text:
Operation Failure
Reclamation reports that every additional 1 foot of decline at Lake Powell equates to a loss of 3 MW of generating capacity; average annual hydropower generation fell from 4,600 GWh (pre-2000) to 3,800 GWh (2000-2020), then to 3,351 GWh in 2021 and 2,590 GWh in 2022.
This quantifies the direct operational consequence of declining Lake Powell storage on hydropower output, showing an accelerating decline through 2022.
source_locators: extracted text; Water Year 2023 Status section

index_text:
Operation Failure
One study estimated that at a Lake Powell elevation of 3,430 feet, the River Outlets would only be able to discharge 10,200 cfs (7.41 MAF/year), considerably less than the Law of the River's requirement of 8.23 MAF/year, and that below the River Outlets' elevation of 3,370 feet, approximately 1.89 MAF would be left as inaccessible dead storage.
This quantifies the specific low-elevation scenario at which Glen Canyon Dam physically cannot meet its downstream delivery obligations, a key operation-failure risk for compact compliance.
source_locators: extracted text; Colorado River Regulation section

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
Pursuant to the 1922 Colorado River Compact and the 1944 Mexican Water Treaty, the Upper Basin must bypass an average of at least 8.25 million acre-feet per year through Glen Canyon Dam to the Lower Basin.
This is the combined Compact-plus-Treaty delivery obligation that Glen Canyon Dam's release capacity is measured against in every low-storage risk scenario.
source_locators: extracted text; Background on Federal Development of the Colorado River Basin section

index_text:
Emergency Operations
On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk of damage from low reservoir levels.
This documents a real, dated 2026 emergency operational decision responding to critically low Lake Powell storage, distinct from earlier planning documents' hypothetical scenarios.
source_locators: extracted text; article opening paragraphs

index_text:
Emergency Operations
With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation will release between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the April 2026 announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23.
This is a specific, quantified 2026 upstream drawdown action comparable in kind but larger in scale than the 2021-2022 DROA transfers documented in CRS-002.
source_locators: extracted text; article body

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
In April 2026, Reclamation invoked its Section 6(E) authority for the first time, using it to cut Lake Powell's water releases from 7.48 million acre-feet to 6 million acre-feet.
This documents the first-ever use of a specific statutory authority to force a large, unilateral reduction in Lake Powell releases.
source_locators: extracted text; article body

index_text:
Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
As of April 2026, Lake Powell's elevation sat at 3,526 feet; Reclamation stated it would try to prevent the reservoir from dropping below 3,500 feet, since hydropower generation stops at 3,490 feet, a level projected to be breached by August 2026 without the announced interventions.
This is a concrete, dated snapshot of Lake Powell's elevation relative to its critical operating thresholds at a moment of acute drought stress.
source_locators: extracted text; article body

index_text:
Inflow Forecast
Inflows into Lake Powell in 2026 are projected to be the lowest ever measured, breaking the previous record set in 2002, driven by a downward snowpack trend and a March 2026 heat wave that was the most extreme on record in the Southwest for that time of year.
This is a current, record-setting inflow forecast directly explaining why Reclamation took emergency action in April 2026.
source_locators: extracted text; article body

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
Cutting Lake Powell outflows to 6 million acre-feet in 2026 will likely push the required 10-year aggregate Lee Ferry delivery total below the Colorado River Compact's 75-million-acre-foot threshold (roughly 82.5 million acre-feet including Mexico's share), raising the prospect of first-ever interstate lawsuits over Colorado River supply.
This directly links a 2026 Lake Powell release reduction to a specific, quantified Compact-compliance risk and potential litigation among Basin states.
source_locators: extracted text; article body

index_text:
Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
At Glen Canyon Dam, minimum power pool is elevation 3,490 feet, which is 20 feet above the generators' penstock intakes; the dam's eight turbines must be shut down at minimum power pool to avoid cavitation.
Explains why the 3,490-foot elevation, not the physical intake elevation itself, is the operational trigger for shutting down hydropower generation.
source_locators: extracted text; main article body

index_text:
Emergency Operations
Below minimum power pool, the only remaining way to pass water through Glen Canyon Dam is the river outlet works (bypass tubes): two intakes leading to four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes with a combined maximum discharge capacity of 15,000 cubic feet per second.
Quantifies the drastically reduced backup release capacity (15,000 cfs vs. 33,000 cfs through the penstocks) available once normal hydropower releases are no longer possible.
source_locators: extracted text; main article body

index_text:
Operation Failure
In 2023, when the river outlet works were used to conduct a high-flow release into the Grand Canyon at low-reservoir levels, damaging cavitation occurred, and the Bureau has warned that further extended use would likely cause more.
Demonstrates that the outlet works' theoretical backup capacity may not be reliably usable for sustained periods at low storage, undermining its role as a fallback release mechanism.
source_locators: extracted text; main article body

index_text:
Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
If Lake Powell drops to the river outlet works' elevation of 3,370 feet, the reservoir reaches “dead pool,” at which water passes through the dam only when river flow exceeds evaporation losses, with no lower intakes or spillways available.
Marks the absolute floor of controllable releases from Glen Canyon Dam, below which downstream water delivery becomes physically impossible except by natural overflow.
source_locators: extracted text; main article body

index_text:
Stakeholders
California, Arizona, and Nevada warned in a letter to the Interior Secretary that Reclamation's failure to address Glen Canyon Dam's infrastructure limitations in the current post-2026 operations EIS is against federal law.
Signals a formal Lower Basin state objection that infrastructure risk, not just water allocation, must be addressed within the ongoing post-2026 NEPA process.
source_locators: extracted text; main article body

index_text:
Operation Rules
A "Normal Condition" for Lake Mead exists in years when its January 1 elevation is projected to be above 1,075 feet and below 1,145 feet, in which case the Secretary determines either a Normal Condition or, per Section 2.B.5, an ICS Surplus Condition.
Defines the baseline elevation band under which standard 7.5 maf Lower Basin deliveries occur without shortage or surplus adjustments.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 2.A Normal Conditions

index_text:
Operation Rules
When Lake Mead content is projected at or below elevation 1,075 feet and at or above 1,050 feet on January 1, a Shortage Condition apportions 7.167 maf for Lower Division consumptive use, split 2.48 maf Arizona, 287,000 af Nevada, and 4.4 maf California.
This is the first (mildest) numeric shortage tier defined by the Interim Guidelines, directly linking a Lake Mead elevation band to a specific reduced delivery volume.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 2.D.1.a Shortage Conditions

index_text:
Operation Rules
When Lake Mead content is projected below elevation 1,050 feet and at or above 1,025 feet on January 1, the Shortage Condition apportions 7.083 maf for Lower Division consumptive use, split 2.4 maf Arizona, 283,000 af Nevada, and 4.4 maf California.
Defines the second, deeper numeric shortage tier, showing how Arizona and Nevada absorb progressively larger reductions as Lake Mead declines while California's apportionment stays fixed at 4.4 maf.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 2.D.1.b Shortage Conditions

index_text:
Operation Rules
When Lake Mead content is projected below elevation 1,025 feet on January 1, the deepest Shortage Condition tier apportions only 7.0 maf for Lower Division consumptive use, split 2.32 maf Arizona, 280,000 af Nevada, and 4.4 maf California.
This is the most severe of the three original shortage tiers, representing the guideline's floor-level delivery reduction before the Lower Elevation Balancing Tier at Lake Powell also engages.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 2.D.1.c Shortage Conditions

index_text:
Operation Rules
In the Upper Elevation Balancing Tier (Lake Powell projected January 1 elevation below the Equalization Elevation Table value and at or above 3,575 feet), the Secretary releases 8.23 maf from Lake Powell if Lake Mead's January 1 elevation is at or above 1,075 feet; if Lake Mead is below 1,075 feet, releases are balanced between not less than 7.0 and not more than 9.0 maf.
This is the core coordinated-operations tier rule that ties Lake Powell's annual release volume directly to both reservoirs' elevations rather than a fixed volume.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 6.B Upper Elevation Balancing Tier

index_text:
Operation Rules
In the Mid-Elevation Release Tier (Lake Powell January 1 elevation projected below 3,575 feet and at or above 3,525 feet), the Secretary releases 7.48 maf from Lake Powell if Lake Mead's January 1 elevation is at or above 1,025 feet, or 8.23 maf if Lake Mead is below 1,025 feet.
This tier and its 7.48 maf default release value is the operating rule directly referenced in the 2026 24-Month Study as governing current-year Lake Powell operations.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 6.C Mid-Elevation Release Tier

index_text:
Operation Rules
In the Lower Elevation Balancing Tier (Lake Powell January 1 elevation projected below 3,525 feet), the Secretary balances the contents of Lake Mead and Lake Powell but releases not more than 9.5 maf and not less than 7.0 maf from Lake Powell in the Water Year.
This is the most severe coordinated-operations tier, engaging when Lake Powell drops below the 3,525-foot Target Elevation referenced elsewhere in the DCP framework.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 6.D Lower Elevation Balancing Tier

index_text:
Operation Rules
If Lake Powell reaches the elevation stated in the Lake Powell Equalization Elevation Table for a given Water Year and the September 30 projected Lake Mead elevation is below 1,105 feet, the Secretary releases additional water from Lake Powell to Lake Mead until the reservoirs fully equalize, Lake Mead reaches 1,105 feet, or Lake Powell reaches 20 feet below its equalization elevation.
This is the Equalization Tier stop-condition rule governing how much extra water is released to prevent Lake Mead from falling too far below Lake Powell in high-storage years.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 6.A Equalization Tier

index_text:
Uncertainty and Risk Management
Whenever Lake Mead is below elevation 1,025 feet, the Secretary must consult annually with the Basin States on whether hydrologic conditions and anticipated deliveries are likely to cause Lake Mead to fall below 1,000 feet, and must implement any additional measures consistent with applicable federal law.
Establishes a mandatory risk-escalation consultation trigger tied to a specific elevation threshold well below the standard shortage tiers, anticipating conditions more severe than those explicitly addressed by the numeric shortage volumes.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 7.B.4 Consultation

index_text:
Stakeholders
If monthly 24-Month Study projections indicate Lake Mead elevations may approach an elevation that would trigger shortages, the Secretary must consult with the Department of State, USIBWC, and Basin States on whether and how the United States may reduce the quantity of water allotted to Mexico consistent with the 1944 Treaty.
Shows that Lake Powell/Mead shortage-tier projections carry international treaty implications requiring formal binational consultation, not just domestic Basin State coordination.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 7.B.3 Consultation

index_text:
Uncertainty and Risk Management
From October 1, 1999 through September 30, 2007, Colorado River reservoir storage fell from 55.8 maf (approximately 94 percent of capacity) to 32.1 maf (approximately 54 percent of capacity), and was as low as 29.7 maf (approximately 52 percent) in 2004 - the worst eight-year drought in over a century of recordkeeping, which directly motivated the Interim Guidelines.
Provides the quantitative hydrologic-risk baseline that justified creating explicit shortage tiers and coordinated operations rules for Lake Powell and Lake Mead.
source_locators: extracted text; Section III Background

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
A "Shortage Condition" is legally defined as existing when the Secretary determines insufficient mainstream water is available to satisfy 7.5 maf of annual consumptive use in the Lower Division states (Arizona, California, Nevada); prior to adoption of the Interim Guidelines, the Secretary had never made such a determination.
Establishes the statutory/administrative definition of Shortage that the numeric tier rules in Section 2.D operationalize, and confirms shortages were a new, previously undeclared operating condition as of 2007.
source_locators: extracted text; Section III Background

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
The Interim Guidelines are implemented by the Secretary each year through the Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (established pursuant to the Colorado River Basin Project Act of 1968), issued via the Annual Operating Plan, and would remain in effect for determinations made through 2025 regarding operations through 2026.
Identifies the statutory chain of authority and annual issuance mechanism (LROC/AOP) through which the Interim Guidelines' elevation-tier rules are actually applied to Lake Powell operations each year.
source_locators: extracted text; Section II Decision

index_text:
Multiple Objectives
The proposed federal action's purpose was to improve Reclamation's management of the Colorado River by weighing trade-offs between the frequency and magnitude of water delivery reductions and the effects on water storage in Lake Powell and Lake Mead, water supply, power production, recreation, and other environmental resources.
Confirms the Interim Guidelines were explicitly designed to balance multiple competing objectives (delivery reliability, storage protection, power, recreation, environment) rather than optimizing a single operational goal.
source_locators: extracted text; Section IV Alternatives Considered

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
The 2007 Interim Guidelines, anticipated to remain in place through 2026, provide operating criteria for Lake Powell and Lake Mead that give water users greater certainty about the timing and volume of potential water delivery reductions.
States the core governance purpose of the 2007 Interim Guidelines that this 2024 ROD amends rather than replaces.
source_locators: extracted text; I. Introduction

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
The 2024 Record of Decision's central action is to adjust the 2007 Interim Guidelines for Lower Basin shortages and coordinated operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead, as codified in Section IX of the 2024 ROD.
This is the formal decision statement establishing that the 2024 ROD amends, rather than replaces, the governing 2007 framework.
source_locators: extracted text; II. Decision

index_text:
Operation Rules
The Preferred Alternative in the 2024 near-term ROD set a target of 3.0 million acre-feet of additional SEIS conservation through 2026, with a minimum of 1.5 MAF physically conserved by the end of calendar year 2024.
This is the quantified near-term conservation target Reclamation and the Lower Basin states must meet under the 2024 ROD, separate from existing 2007 Interim Guideline and DCP shortage volumes.
source_locators: extracted text; IV. Alternatives Considered, B. Preferred Alternative

index_text:
Operation Rules
Under the 2024 ROD's new Section XI.G.6.E, if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 feet at Lake Powell in the next 12 months, the Secretary must begin planning to reduce Lake Powell releases as needed to not less than 6.0 MAF for the Water Year to maintain elevation 3,500 feet.
This is the specific new if/then rule added by the 2024 ROD that converts a 24-Month Study elevation projection into a mandatory release-reduction planning action.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 6.E, Mid-Elevation and Lower Elevation Balancing Tiers

index_text:
Emergency Operations
Whenever Lake Mead's content is projected to fall below elevation 1,025 feet based on the April 24-Month Study minimum probable projection, the Lower Division States, after consulting the Upper Division States, have 45 calendar days to provide Reclamation an implementation plan to protect Lake Mead from reaching elevation 1,000 feet.
This is a defined-timeline emergency coordination requirement that forces state-level action planning before Lake Mead approaches a critically low elevation.
source_locators: extracted text; IV. Alternatives Considered, B. Preferred Alternative

index_text:
Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
Dry hydrology in recent years produced low Lake Powell elevations at levels such as 3,490 feet, Glen Canyon Dam's minimum power pool, giving Reclamation operating experience it is using to refine facility operating parameters.
Shows Reclamation is treating recent low-elevation operating experience as direct input for refining future operating parameters rather than a one-off event.
source_locators: extracted text; VII.B. Operational Considerations

index_text:
Uncertainty and Risk Management
The period from 2000 through 2022 is the driest 23-year period in more than a century and one of the driest periods in the last 1,200 years in the Colorado River Basin.
This drought-severity statistic is the ROD's stated basis for concluding that the 2007 Interim Guidelines needed near-term supplemental adjustment.
source_locators: extracted text; III. Background

index_text:
Emergency Operations
Reclamation's Interim Operating Guidance for Glen Canyon Dam during Low Reservoir Levels directs Reclamation to exercise the full extent of operational capabilities within the Upper Colorado Basin to attempt to maintain reservoir level at or above elevation 3,490 feet, minimum power pool.
This is the specific emergency-response guidance document instructing Reclamation to use all available Upper Basin tools to defend the minimum power pool elevation.
source_locators: extracted text; VII.B. Operational Considerations

index_text:
Modeling
Under the Preferred Alternative, hydrologic ensemble modeling projected the percentage of traces with Lake Powell falling below elevation 3,490 feet at 0 percent in 2024 and 2025 and 2 percent in 2026.
Quantifies the modeled probability of hitting the minimum power pool threshold under the adopted alternative, providing a numeric risk baseline for the 2024-2026 period.
source_locators: extracted text; VII.B. Operational Considerations

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
In 2024, in response to the SEIS purpose and need, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service issued a new Biological Opinion for the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program allowing annual flow reductions in a range of 2.083 MAF up to 3.0 MAF through January 2028.
This ESA compliance action is what legally enables implementation of the reduced Lower Basin flow volumes contemplated in the Preferred Alternative.
source_locators: extracted text; VIII.A. Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program

index_text:
Stakeholders
Additional operating decisions made through the 2024 ROD are coordinated through the Colorado River Management Workgroup, which includes representatives from Basin States, Basin Tribes, Mexico, and other partners.
Identifies the standing multi-party coordination body responsible for operational notification and consultation under the new ROD provisions.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 7.B. Consultation

index_text:
Regulation / Governance
DOI selected Alternative D without modification as the governing 20-year operating and adaptive-management framework for Glen Canyon Dam, identifying it in the ROD as both the preferred and the environmentally preferred alternative from among seven alternatives analyzed in the LTEMP FEIS.
This is the binding governance decision that establishes which operating framework legally governs Glen Canyon Dam releases and experiments for the following 20 years.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 1. SUMMARY OF ACTION

index_text:
Operation Purposes
The LTEMP's stated purpose is to provide a comprehensive framework for adaptively managing Glen Canyon Dam operations over the next 20 years, consistent with the Grand Canyon Protection Act (GCPA), to determine dam operations and actions that improve downstream conditions while continuing to meet water delivery and hydropower obligations.
This purpose statement defines the operating objective against which the selected alternative and all subsequent experimental actions are justified.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 2. PURPOSE AND NEED

index_text:
Operation Rules
The selected alternative defines monthly release-volume schedules for ten discrete total-annual-release levels ranging from 7,000 to 14,000 thousand acre-feet (Table 1), with in-year monthly operations subject to increase or decrease based on operational-flexibility and experimental-implementation factors described elsewhere in the ROD.
This tiered monthly-volume schedule is the core operating rule translating annual Colorado River Basin hydrology into specific monthly Glen Canyon Dam release targets.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 1, Table 1 Monthly Release Volumes of the Selected Alternative

index_text:
Operation Rules
Under Alternative D base operations, the allowable within-day flow fluctuation range is set proportionally to the month's scheduled release volume: 10 times the monthly volume (in kaf) in the high-demand months of June, July, and August, and 9 times the monthly volume in other months, subject to an overall cap.
This proportional fluctuation formula directly links hourly hydropower load-following flexibility to the monthly release schedule, replacing a flat rule with a volume-scaled one.
source_locators: extracted text; Attachment B Section 1.1 Base Operations Under Alternative D

index_text:
Operation Rules
Alternative D sets the down-ramp rate at Glen Canyon Dam at no more than 2,500 cfs/hr (1,000 cfs/hr greater than under the No-Action Alternative) while retaining the up-ramp rate at 4,000 cfs/hr, the same as under the No-Action Alternative.
The relaxed down-ramp rate increases operational efficiency and flexibility for hydropower load-following while the up-ramp limit is unchanged, showing a targeted, asymmetric rule adjustment.
source_locators: extracted text; Attachment B Section 1.1 Base Operations Under Alternative D

index_text:
Operation Rules
The 8,000 cfs maximum daily fluctuation limit retained under Alternative D was originally established in the 1996 ROD to address safety, recreation, and sediment concerns, and was based on river-guide survey preferences for a tolerable recreation experience.
This shows the daily fluctuation cap is a long-standing, evidence-based operating constraint carried forward across RODs rather than a new restriction, anchoring current operations to a 1987 recreation study.
source_locators: extracted text; Attachment B Section 1.1 Base Operations Under Alternative D

index_text:
Real-Time Operations
Reclamation conducts monthly Glen Canyon Dam operational coordination meetings or calls with DOI bureaus (USGS, NPS, FWS, BIA), WAPA, and one liaison from each Basin State and the UCRC to share and obtain up-to-date information on dam operations and resource status.
This recurring monthly coordination process is the operational mechanism by which near-term release decisions and resource conditions are communicated among all operating and stakeholder entities.
source_locators: extracted text; Attachment B Section 1.1 Base Operations Under Alternative D

index_text:
Uncertainty and Risk Management
Reclamation retains authority for operational flexibility at Glen Canyon Dam specifically because hydrologic and reservoir conditions across the Colorado River Basin cannot be completely known in advance, permitting in-year adjustments to daily and monthly release volumes for water-distribution, resource-related, and hydropower-related reasons.
This is the explicit rule-level acknowledgment that hydrologic uncertainty requires a built-in operational flexibility mechanism rather than a fixed release schedule.
source_locators: extracted text; Attachment B Section 1.2 Operational Flexibility Under Alternative D

index_text:
Emergency Operations

Operation Rules
Under Alternative D's updated High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol, spring and fall HFE releases (1 to 250 hours long, 31,500 to 45,000 cfs) are triggered by the modeled sand mass balance from Paria River sediment inputs during defined spring (Dec 1-Jun 30) and fall (Jul 1-Nov 30) accounting periods, and extended-duration fall HFEs (>96 hr) are capped at four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period.

Operation Rules
Extended-duration fall HFEs will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume, meaning water-delivery constraints can override an otherwise-triggered extended HFE test.

Operation Rules
Trout Management Flows (TMFs) under Alternative D consist of repeated fluctuation cycles combining sustained high flows (e.g., 20,000 cfs) with a rapid drop to a very low flow (e.g., 5,000-8,000 cfs) intended to strand young-of-year trout; up to three TMF cycles per month may be tested over as many as four months (May-August).

Operation Rules

Operation Rules

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
Glen Canyon Dam, completed in 1963, is the second-highest concrete-arch dam in the United States and created Lake Powell with more than 26 million acre-feet of water storage capacity.

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
Lake Powell has a maximum live storage capacity of about 24.3 maf and Glen Canyon Dam is designed to operate between the outlet works intake elevation of 3,370 ft AMSL and the top of the live storage pool at 3,700 ft AMSL; hydropower production ceases if the reservoir drops below the minimum power pool elevation of approximately 3,490 ft.

Operation Rules
The Interim Guidelines for Coordinated Operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead define four operating tiers -- Equalization Tier, Upper Elevation Balancing Tier, Mid-Elevation Release Tier, and Lower Elevation Balancing Tier -- with scheduled Lake Powell water-year releases adjusted each month based on forecast inflow and projected September 30 elevations at both reservoirs.

Operation Rules
Under the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) regime from the 1996 ROD, Glen Canyon Dam release rates must be 8,000 cfs or greater between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. and at least 5,000 cfs at night, and ramp rates are capped at 4,000 cfs/hr for increases (up-ramp) and 1,500 cfs/hr for decreases (down-ramp).
These are the binding minimum-flow and ramp-rate rules that constrain daily dam operations and downstream fluctuation zones under the current baseline regime.

Operation Rules
MLFF allowable daily flow fluctuation is tiered by monthly release volume: 5,000 cfs/day when monthly release is under 600 kaf, 6,000 cfs/day for 600-800 kaf, and 8,000 cfs/day when monthly release is 800 kaf or higher.

Operation Rules
Under MLFF the maximum release for power generation is capped at 25,000 cfs, well below the eight turbines' maximum combined discharge capacity of approximately 31,500 cfs, limiting Glen Canyon Powerplant to about 1,000 MW (76% of unrestricted usable capacity) at reservoir elevation 3,700 ft.
This gap between the physical release/generation capacity and the rule-imposed cap quantifies the operational and economic cost of environmental constraints on hydropower.

Emergency Operations
Under very wet hydrologic conditions, defined as an average monthly release rate above 25,000 cfs, Glen Canyon Dam may exceed the 25,000 cfs cap but must release at a constant rate; the 25,000 cfs limit may also be exceeded to avoid spills, during flood releases, for approved experimental HFE releases, or to accommodate electrical emergencies.
This describes the specific hydrologic and emergency conditions under which normal MLFF release limits are formally overridden.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 3.13.1.3 Operational Flexibility

Operation Failure
Bypassing water around the Glen Canyon powerplant generators (e.g., during HFEs or high releases beyond turbine capacity) produces no hydroelectric energy, forces WAPA to purchase replacement power, and raises tailwater stage, which reduces effective head and power-conversion efficiency at the turbines.
This documents a concrete operational limitation: any release exceeding turbine capacity has cascading economic and efficiency costs rather than simply passing through as generation.
source_locators: extracted text; Section 3.13.1.3 Operational Flexibility

Operation Failure
MLFF ramping restrictions prevent Glen Canyon Dam generation from adjusting hourly to match power customer demand, forcing increased reliance on alternate generating resources; between 1997 and 2005 this operational restriction cost WAPA and its power customers an average of $38 million to $50 million per year.
This quantifies the direct economic cost of the environmentally motivated operating constraints, a key tradeoff cited throughout the LTEMP power-operations discussion.

Real-Time Operations
Glen Canyon Dam's load/generation-following regulation capability, used by WAPA to balance instantaneous changes in load or generation within its Balancing Authority, is limited to plus or minus 40 MW and operates outside the 1996 ROD ramping restrictions.
This defines the narrow real-time regulation band the dam can use for grid balancing independent of the daily ramp-rate rules that otherwise govern releases.

Real-Time Operations
Beyond the formal ROD requirements, WAPA follows discretionary dispatch practices at Glen Canyon Dam -- such as holding nightly generation to the same minimum level during off-peak hours and keeping weekend releases at no less than 85% of the average weekday release -- that fall within MLFF constraints but are not ROD requirements and can be altered or abandoned at any time.
This shows that some day-to-day release patterns are operator discretion rather than fixed regulatory rule, meaning actual near-term operations can shift without a formal rule change.

Emergency Operations
NERC contingency reserve standards require that a sudden generation loss or transmission imbalance (a disturbance) be corrected within 10 minutes; Glen Canyon Dam's reserve capacity is also contractually used to restart tripped thermal powerplants and provide emergency shutdown power to nuclear powerplants, and responding to such electrical emergencies is exempt from 1996 ROD operating constraints.
This documents a defined emergency-response obligation and threshold (10 minutes) that overrides normal release rules and ties Glen Canyon Dam's flexibility to regional grid and nuclear-safety reliability.

Lake Powell's hydraulic retention time is about 2 years, based on an active reservoir capacity of roughly 24 million acre-feet and an average annual inflow of about 11 million acre-feet; year-to-year retention time has historically ranged between about 1 and 5 years.

Lake Powell develops thermal stratification into epilimnion, metalimnion, and hypolimnion layers each year, beginning in spring and typically stable by July, persisting until autumn air temperatures drop and surface cooling drives vertical mixing back toward isothermal conditions.

Trout management flows (TMFs) -- an experimental release pattern of roughly 20,000 ft3/s for 2-7 days followed by a rapid drop to 5,000-8,000 ft3/s -- are designed to strand young-of-year rainbow trout, trading rainbow trout fishery quality against reduced downstream emigration risk to humpback chub; TMFs had never been implemented at Glen Canyon Dam as of this report.

Future inflow uncertainty for the LTEMP analysis was modeled using the indexed sequential method to resample the 105-year historical natural flow record (1906-2010), selecting every fifth trace to produce 21 hydrological traces; every long-term strategy was evaluated against all 21 traces.

Inflow Forecast

Modeling
A total of 10 modeling teams built a linked suite of simulation models -- including CRSS/RiverWare for monthly volumes and reservoir elevations, GTMax-Lite for daily/hourly flow and hydropower generation, a sand budget model for sediment transport, a CE-QUAL-W2 water temperature model, and a coupled rainbow trout-humpback chub population model -- to forecast performance of the 19 long-term strategies against the 18 performance metrics.

Uncertainty and Risk Management
Critical uncertainties about trout-management-flow effectiveness (10 percent versus 50 percent reduction in rainbow trout recruitment) and the effect of fall HFEs on rainbow trout recruitment (no effect versus an effect equivalent to spring HFEs but for one year) were quantified through a four-person fish-biologist expert panel using a modified Delphi four-point elicitation process convened in March 2014.

Operation Rules
Using the joint-lead agencies' average stakeholder weighting, long-term strategy D4 (under Alternative D) had the highest weighted performance across the 18 metrics; alternatives C, D, E, F, and G all substantially outperformed status-quo Alternative A provided HFEs were implemented, while long-term strategies that omitted HFEs (C3, E3, E5, and E6) performed worse than the status quo.

index_text:
Uncertainty and Risk Management
The expected value of perfect information for resolving the critical scientific uncertainties (fall HFE effect on trout, TMF effectiveness, temperature-versus-trout effect on humpback chub) was essentially zero for nearly all stakeholder weightings -- the same best-performing long-term strategy was identified across all 16 combinations of competing hypotheses for 12 of 14 stakeholders, and the two exceptions had an EVPI of less than 0.1 percent.
A central and counterintuitive finding of the decision analysis: resolving the ecological uncertainties long debated within the Adaptive Management Program would not change which LTEMP long-term strategy is preferred, reducing the urgency of further experimentation on those specific questions.
