Emergency Operations
What flood-frequency-reduction commitment governs unanticipated floods exceeding 45,000 cfs at Glen Canyon Dam, and how is it achieved?
Under the 1996 ROD's Flood Frequency Reduction Measures, the frequency of unanticipated floods exceeding 45,000 cfs is to be reduced to an average of once in 100 years, accomplished initially through the Annual Operating Plan process and eventually by raising Glen Canyon Dam's spillway gates 4.5 feet (EU-LP-OFF-008-05). The 2002 Report to Congress restates the identical commitment: the frequency of unanticipated flood flows exceeding 45,000 cfs will be reduced to no more than 1 year in 100 years as a long-term average, using the same two-phase approach -- Annual Operating Plan process, then a 4.5-foot spillway gate raise (EU-LP-OFF-009-07).

Emergency Operations
Under what conditions may Glen Canyon Dam exceed the normal 25,000 cfs maximum release limit?
Under the 2016 LTEMP FEIS, when very wet hydrologic conditions occur (average monthly release rate above 25,000 cfs), Glen Canyon Dam may exceed the 25,000 cfs cap but must release at a constant rate; the limit may also be exceeded to avoid spills, during flood releases, for approved experimental high-flow-experiment (HFE) releases, or to accommodate electrical emergencies (EU-LP-OFF-005-06). Consistent with this, the 2007 Biological Assessment states the 25,000 cfs maximum flow limit under the 1996 ROD and 1997 Operating Criteria may be exceeded for emergency conditions and during extreme hydrological conditions, and notes that separate emergency exception criteria also apply during normal operations (EU-LP-OFF-011-16).

Emergency Operations
What are the Emergency Exception Criteria that allow Glen Canyon Dam to deviate from normal operating rules during emergencies, and what situations do they cover?
The Emergency Exception Criteria were established under Section 3 of the Glen Canyon Dam Operating Criteria (62 FR 9448, March 3, 1997) and continue unchanged under LTEMP Alternative D; when invoked, normal operations are suspended until the emergency has ended or WAPA has discharged its NERC responsibility regarding the emergency (EU-LP-OFF-003-09). The 1996 ROD establishes that these criteria allow WAPA to respond to various emergency situations consistent with its North American Electric Reliability Council (NERC) obligations, with exceptions to standard operating criteria during search-and-rescue situations, special studies and monitoring, dam and powerplant maintenance, and spinning reserves (EU-LP-OFF-008-06). GAO's 1997 assessment describes these deviations as usually lasting less than 4 hours, covering power and water emergencies such as insufficient generating capacity, restoration of the electrical system, or search-and-rescue operations (EU-LP-OFF-010-05). The underlying NERC standard requires a disturbance (sudden generation loss or transmission imbalance) be corrected within 10 minutes; Glen Canyon Dam's reserve capacity is also contractually used to restart tripped thermal powerplants and provide emergency shutdown power to nuclear powerplants, and responding to such electrical emergencies is exempt from 1996 ROD operating constraints (EU-LP-OFF-005-11).

Emergency Operations
What is the Drought Response Operations Agreement's (DROA) protective elevation target for Lake Powell, and how is it triggered and implemented?
Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

Emergency Operations
What specific upstream reservoir releases did Reclamation implement under the DROA in 2021-2022 to protect Lake Powell's elevation?
CRS R47497 states that in 2021 Reclamation transferred 180,000 acre-feet to Lake Powell from Flaming Gorge (125,000 AF), Blue Mesa (36,000 AF), and Navajo (20,000 AF) reservoirs, and in 2022 reduced Lake Powell releases from 7.48 to 7.00 maf while transferring an additional 0.50 maf from Flaming Gorge (EU-LP-CRS-002-05). Reclamation's own DROA program page states that beginning summer 2021, pursuant to the DROA, Reclamation determined an imminent need to release 161,000 acre-feet from the upstream Flaming Gorge and Aspinall Unit (Blue Mesa) Initial Units, and that in January 2022 it additionally modified Glen Canyon Dam releases, readjusting 350,000 acre-feet, to protect critical elevations at Lake Powell (EU-LP-OFF-031-03). The two sources give different acre-foot totals for what appears to be overlapping 2021-2022 DROA-triggered actions (180,000 AF vs. 161,000 AF for 2021; a 0.50 maf Flaming Gorge transfer vs. a 350,000 AF Glen Canyon Dam release readjustment for 2022), and neither source alone clarifies whether these figures represent the same actions counted differently, partial vs. final tallies, or genuinely distinct actions.

Emergency Operations
What emergency drought-response actions did Reclamation take in 2026 to protect Lake Powell from falling to critically low elevation?
On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk from low reservoir levels (EU-LP-MED-001-01). With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation committed to releasing between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23 (EU-LP-MED-001-02). Because WY2026 was historically dry and Lake Powell was projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-023-02). Reclamation's newsroom release confirms the combined plan: adding about 2.48 million acre-feet via the 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge release (April 2026-April 2027, under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements) plus the 7.48-to-6.0-maf release reduction through September 2026 under Section 6E, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet to at least 3,500 feet by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-035-02).

Emergency Operations
What shortage-tier condition governs Lake Mead and Colorado River deliveries in calendar year 2026, and what contributions does it require?
A Shortage Condition governs Lake Mead operations for calendar year 2026 under Section 2.D.1.a of the 2007 Interim Guidelines and Article III(3)(c) of the Operating Criteria, with DCP contributions required from Arizona and Nevada consistent with the Lower Basin DCP Agreement (EU-LP-OFF-022-12). Specifically, this is a Level 1 Shortage Condition, with Lake Mead projected at elevation 1,055.88 feet (20 feet below the Lower Basin shortage-determination trigger), requiring Arizona to contribute 512,000 acre-feet (18 percent of its apportionment), Nevada 21,000 acre-feet (7 percent), and Mexico 80,000 acre-feet (5 percent) (EU-LP-OFF-036-02).

Emergency Operations
What is the Glen Canyon Dam high-flow-experiment (HFE) protocol established since 2012, and what triggers its implementation?
High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring (EU-LP-RES-014-05). This decision-making protocol, approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012, coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary (EU-LP-RES-018-01). Across the full historical record, 11 HFEs were released from Glen Canyon Dam between 1996 and November 2018, with peak magnitudes ranging from 864 to 1,274 cubic meters per second and durations from 24 to 168 hours, including lower-magnitude habitat maintenance flows (HMFs) in 1997 and 2000 (EU-LP-RES-018-02).

Emergency Operations
What were the specifics and outcome of the 1996 Glen Canyon Dam controlled-flood (first HFE) experiment?
In spring 1996 Reclamation conducted its first controlled-flood (beach/habitat-building) experiment, ramping releases from a steady 8,000 cfs baseline up to a peak of 45,000 cfs (approximately 1,274 cubic meters per second) held for 7 days beginning March 26, 1996, before stepping back down; preliminary results showed sandbars in the Glen and Grand canyons increased by as much as 30 percent and numerous new backwaters were created for fish (EU-LP-OFF-010-14). The 1996 HFE's major objective was to determine whether high releases from Glen Canyon Dam could effectively redistribute sand from the riverbed to the channel margins; because it followed two years of below-average tributary sand input, suspended sediment progressively coarsened and depleted during the event (EU-LP-RES-018-08).

Real-Time Operations
What non-native fish suppression flow pattern was implemented at Glen Canyon Dam during 2003-2005, and what were its parameters?
As part of the 2002-2004 experimental program, Reclamation implemented non-native fish suppression releases from Glen Canyon Dam with daily fluctuations of 5,000-20,000 cfs during January 1-March 31 of 2003, continuing this high-fluctuation suppression flow pattern in 2004 and 2005 to test its effectiveness at limiting non-native fish recruitment (EU-LP-OFF-011-14). Consistent with this, non-native fish suppression flows with daily fluctuations between 142 and 566 cubic meters per second -- the metric equivalent of 5,000-20,000 cfs -- were released each January through March from 2003 to 2005, representing a departure from the standard LTEMP/MLFF flow regime (EU-LP-RES-018-06).

Emergency Operations
What was Glen Canyon Dam's original design flood, and how was reservoir storage used to reduce the required spillway discharge?
Glen Canyon Dam's spillways were designed to pass a maximum probable snowmelt flood with a predicted peak discharge of 380,000 cfs and a volume of 29,060,000 acre-feet over a 4-month period, about 1.7 times the maximum recorded historical discharge of 220,000 cfs (EU-LP-OFF-027-05). Under the design flood-routing scenario, storing approximately 1,850,000 acre-feet of the floodwater and allowing the reservoir to rise to elevation 3,711 feet would limit the maximum discharge through the spillways to 276,000 cfs (EU-LP-OFF-027-06).

Stakeholders
What is the Ten Tribes Partnership, and what is the scale of its reserved Colorado River water rights?
The Ten Tribes Partnership was formed in 1992 by ten federally recognized tribes with federal Indian reserved water rights or claims in the Colorado River or its tributaries; the 2018 Tribal Water Study documents their current water use and projects future development (EU-LP-OFF-026-01). Partnership Tribes hold reserved water rights, including unresolved claims, to divert nearly 2.8 million acre-feet of water per year from the Colorado River and its tributaries, but none currently has the infrastructure or legal/administrative flexibility to fully use or realize the economic value of these rights (EU-LP-OFF-026-02).

Emergency Operations
What are Glen Canyon Dam's River Outlet Works, what is their release capacity, and what is known about their historical use and reliability?
The River Outlet Works (bypass tubes) have historically only been opened when the dam was first filled, during short-term high-flow experiments, and for emergency flood releases in the early 1980s, and have never been used over extended periods (EU-LP-CRS-002-03). Below minimum power pool, the River Outlet Works are the only remaining way to pass water through Glen Canyon Dam: two intakes leading to four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes with a combined maximum discharge capacity of 15,000 cubic feet per second (EU-LP-MED-002-02), a capacity figure confirmed on Reclamation's own project page, which also lists a combined spillway discharge capacity of 208,000 cfs at elevation 3,700.0 ft (EU-LP-OFF-030-02). Since the Draft SEIS, Reclamation identified enhanced risks associated with relying on the River Outlet Works as the exclusive means of releasing water at low reservoir elevations for sustained periods, prompting the 2024 Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels (EU-LP-OFF-007-04).

Real-Time Operations
What guidelines govern how Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes are distributed across hours, days, and weeks in normal power operations?
Beyond formal ROD requirements, WAPA follows discretionary dispatch practices at Glen Canyon Dam -- such as holding nightly generation to the same minimum level during off-peak hours and keeping weekend releases at no less than 85 percent of the average weekday release -- that fall within MLFF constraints but are not ROD requirements and can be altered or abandoned by WAPA at any time (EU-LP-OFF-005-10). Per the 1997 GAO report, to the extent possible Glen Canyon Dam's hourly power operations followed three guidelines: maximize water releases during peak energy demand periods (generally Monday-Saturday, 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.); maximize releases during peak-demand months and minimize during low-demand months; and minimize or eliminate powerplant bypasses (EU-LP-OFF-010-13).

Real-Time Operations
What is the Cool Mix Alternative's temperature trigger, and how has it been implemented?
Per the 2024 SEIS, for 2024 implementation the Cool Mix Alternative is triggered when average observed daily water temperature at river mile 61 (Little Colorado River confluence) exceeds 15.5°C (60°F) for three consecutive days, continuing until release temperatures fall back below that threshold at the target location (EU-LP-OFF-007-15). The 2026 Draft Annual Operating Plan describes the Cool Mix Alternative as triggered once average daily water temperature at river mile 30 reaches 15.5°C for three consecutive days, and states it was implemented from July 9 to November 18, 2024 (bypassing approximately 0.894 maf of water) and was reinitiated in August 2025 (EU-LP-OFF-022-09).

Stakeholders
What is the Adaptive Management Work Group (AMWG), who is on it, and what is its authority?
The Glen Canyon Dam Adaptive Management Work Group (AMWG), established in 1997 under the GCDAMP, is a federal advisory committee whose membership includes federal and state resource management agencies, representatives of the seven basin states, American Indian Tribes, hydroelectric power purchase contractors, and environmental/conservation and recreational interest groups (EU-LP-OFF-004-06). Its duties are in an advisory capacity only (EU-LP-OFF-011-12); its recommendations for adjustments to Glen Canyon Dam operations under the Grand Canyon Protection Act are conveyed to the Secretary of the Interior (EU-LP-OFF-012-16).

Modeling
What is the Colorado River Simulation System (CRSS) and what software platform implements it?
CRSS is a package of computer programs and databases, developed over roughly a 10-year period, designed to assist Reclamation in performing comprehensive long-range planning and operations studies of proposed changes to Colorado River operations (impacts on streamflows, floodflows, storage, water allocation deliveries, and basin yields). By 1996, CRSS was fully transitioned from a hardwired Fortran/Cyber mainframe model into the RiverWare software platform, preserving the original model's structure and data while allowing analysts to define and prioritize operating rules through a graphical interface instead of altering source code. In practice, CRSS/RiverWare has been used as one of a linked suite of simulation models (e.g., in the 2015 LTEMP decision analysis) specifically to forecast monthly water volumes and reservoir elevations feeding evaluation of long-term operating strategies.

Modeling
Does CRSS incorporate climate-change-projected flow reductions when generating future Lake Powell elevation projections?
Two independent Reclamation effects analyses -- the 2007 Biological Assessment on Experimental Releases and the 2008 Final Biological Opinion for Glen Canyon Dam operations -- both state that CRSS generates probabilistic projections of future Lake Powell reservoir elevations based on the 100-year historic hydrologic record, rather than on published climate-change flow-reduction projections. The BA additionally attributes this to published climate-change projections not being available at the spatial scale CRSS requires.

Observation and Data
What is the Lees Ferry gaging station and what does its long-term flow record show?
The USGS Lees Ferry gaging station (river mile 0, approximately 15.5-15.9 miles downstream of Glen Canyon Dam) has been operated continuously since May 1921, predating the dam, and serves as the primary long-term Colorado River flow record used for pre-dam/post-dam hydrology comparisons in EIS and planning analyses. Its record shows an average pre-dam annual peak flow of approximately 92,000 cfs, and natural flow at the station has varied annually from about 5.0 to 23.0 million acre-feet.

Observation and Data
What is GCMRC and what is its role in monitoring the effects of Glen Canyon Dam operations?
The USGS Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center (GCMRC) is the designated scientific body providing ongoing monitoring data on the effects of Glen Canyon Dam operations on natural, cultural, and recreational resources, operating as a core component of the Glen Canyon Dam Adaptive Management Program (GCDAMP) alongside the Technical Work Group. Its monitoring covers the Colorado River corridor from the dam forebay through Lees Ferry (approximately 16 river miles) and the entire approximately 277-river-mile corridor downstream within Grand Canyon National Park. Under the LTEMP, GCMRC develops and maintains a dedicated Science Plan that guides ongoing long-term resource monitoring in support of adaptive management.

Modeling
What is Reclamation's 24-Month Study operational model and how is it used to project reservoir operations?
Reclamation's '24-Month Study' is the recurring monthly operational model that projects Colorado River reservoir levels 24 months into the future to inform near-term operating decisions, with each monthly run modeling a single scenario of reservoir conditions. Operationally, projected monthly inflow volumes from probabilistic hydrologic scenarios are input into the 24-Month Study, and the resulting projected monthly releases for each system reservoir are adjusted from the prior month's 24-Month Study baseline until release and storage levels best accomplish project purposes and operational objectives.

Observation and Data
What is the long-term sandbar monitoring network and what has it shown about High-Flow Experiment (HFE) effectiveness?
Glen Canyon Dam's High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol effectiveness is tracked through a network of 45 long-term sandbar monitoring sites, part of a larger repeat topographic/bathymetric survey program (approximately 1,800 surveys) that represents only 7-9 percent of all sandbars in Marble and Grand Canyons but has been shown, by comparison with larger samples, to consistently characterize system-wide average sandbar response. At these 45 sites, sandbars were measured as larger at 52%, 52%, and 57% of sites immediately following the 2012, 2013, and 2014 HFEs respectively, with total sand volume at these sites increasing over the program's first 4 years. For the five HFEs released between 2012 and 2018, pre/post-event topographic surveys were not conducted; instead sandbar response was assessed via daily repeat photographs from remote automated cameras plus annual monitoring surveys collected approximately 11 months after each event.

Modeling
What decision-analysis method was used to evaluate LTEMP operating alternatives/strategies?
Evaluation of Glen Canyon Dam LTEMP operating alternatives used a formal swing-weighting multicriteria decision-analysis (MCDA) process, developed with the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center using the Simple Multi-Attribute Rating Technique (SMART): participating stakeholders ranked and weighted the importance of each performance metric according to its range of effect on resources. This MCDA approach, together with expected-value-of-information (EVPI/EVXI) analysis, was formally used to evaluate 19 long-term strategies against 18 performance metrics and to assess how much uncertainty mattered to the ranking of alternatives. The LTEMP EIS notes this decision-analysis process informed, but was not the sole basis for, selecting the preferred alternative.

Modeling
What is the Colorado River Basin Water Supply and Demand Study (2012) and what future supply-demand imbalance did it project?
The Colorado River Basin Water Supply and Demand Study (conducted January 2010-December 2012) defined current and future imbalances in Colorado River Basin water supply and demand for approximately the next 50 years. Using a scenario-planning process across more than 100 supply sequences per scenario, it found a long-term supply-demand imbalance (10-year running average) ranging from 0 to 6.8 MAF, with a median of 3.2 MAF, projected by 2060. Under the study's demand scenarios, consumptive use demand was projected to range between about 18.1 and 20.4 MAF by 2060, with the largest increase driven by municipal and industrial (M&I) demand growth from population increases, even though agriculture currently accounts for about 70 percent of total Colorado River water used in the U.S.

Observation and Data
What compact-based legal provisions established Colorado River streamflow gaging and data-collection infrastructure?
The legal basis for Colorado River streamflow gaging and data-collection infrastructure was established across two interstate compacts. Article V of the 1922 Colorado River Compact directs the chief water-rights official of each signatory state, together with the Directors of the U.S. Reclamation Service and USGS, to secure the ascertainment and publication of the Colorado River's annual flow at Lee Ferry. The 1948 Upper Colorado River Basin Compact's Article VIII subsequently created the Upper Colorado River Commission (UCRC) and granted it broader authority to locate, establish, and operate water-gaging stations basin-wide, forecast Colorado River runoff, conduct cooperative water-supply studies, and collect, analyze, and report streamflow, storage, diversion, and water-use data.

Operation Rules
What are the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) baseline daily/hourly operating limits (minimum release, maximum release, ramp rates, and daily-fluctuation-by-monthly-volume tiers) that have governed Glen Canyon Dam releases since the 1996 Record of Decision?
Since the 1996 Record of Decision selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) alternative (codified in the 1997 Operating Criteria), Glen Canyon Dam releases have been bound by a consistent set of limits, repeated across CRS reports, LTEMP EIS chapters, biological opinions/assessments, GAO review, and peer-reviewed research: minimum release of 8,000 cfs from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and 5,000 cfs at night; maximum release of 25,000 cfs (well below the approximately 31,500 cfs turbine/penstock capacity, i.e. about 76% of unrestricted capacity at elevation 3,700 ft); ascending (up) ramp rate up to 4,000 cfs/hour; descending (down) ramp rate up to 1,500 cfs/hour; and an allowable daily flow fluctuation that scales with that month's total release volume -- 5,000 cfs/day for monthly release volumes under 0.6 maf (600 kaf), 6,000 cfs/day for 0.6-0.8 maf (600-800 kaf), and 8,000 cfs/day for volumes over 0.8 maf (800 kaf). A peer-reviewed research paper (RES-018) restates the same limits in metric units (141 m3/s minimum, 708 m3/s maximum, and 142/170/227 m3/s daily fluctuation tiers), confirming unit-equivalence with the cfs figures used elsewhere.

Operation Rules
What is the origin and basis of the 8,000 cfs maximum daily fluctuation cap at Glen Canyon Dam, and has it carried forward into the LTEMP preferred alternative?
The 8,000 cfs maximum daily fluctuation limit (the top tier of the MLFF sliding-scale fluctuation rule) was established in the 1996 Record of Decision to address safety, recreation, and sediment concerns, based on a 1995 study (Reclamation 1995) of river-guide/public flow preferences. Under the LTEMP Final EIS (2016), this same 8,000 cfs cap is retained and is present in both the No Action Alternative and the LTEMP preferred alternative (Alternative D).

Operation Rules
What ramp-rate limits and daily-fluctuation formula does LTEMP Alternative D (2016 ROD) apply to Glen Canyon Dam base operations, and how do they differ from the prior MLFF (1996 ROD) values?
Under LTEMP Alternative D (the 2016 ROD selected alternative), the allowable within-day fluctuation range is no longer a fixed 3-tier schedule but a formula proportional to that month's scheduled release volume: 10 x monthly volume (kaf) in June-August, and 9 x monthly volume (kaf) in other months, subject to an overall cap (stated elsewhere as 227 m3/s, approximately 8,000 cfs). Alternative D also raises the down-ramp (descending) rate limit to no more than 2,500 cfs/hour (1,000 cfs/hour greater than the prior No-Action/MLFF limit of 1,500 cfs/hour), while retaining the up-ramp (ascending) rate at 4,000 cfs/hour, unchanged from MLFF. A companion research paper restates these LTEMP ramp rates in metric units: 113 m3/s/hour increasing (~4,000 cfs/hr) and 71 m3/s/hour decreasing (~2,500 cfs/hr), explicitly framed as a change made to reduce sandbar erosion rates.

Operation Rules
What flow magnitude, physical release pathway, and duration define a High-Flow Experiment (HFE) release from Glen Canyon Dam?
High-Flow Experiment (HFE) releases from Glen Canyon Dam are triggered when there is sufficient sediment input from the Paria River and typically range from approximately 30,000 to 45,000 cfs, used to mobilize channel-stored sand and redeposit it as sandbars, beaches, and associated backwater/riparian habitat. An HFE is defined as using full powerplant capacity (30,000 cfs) plus the four bypass (river outlet) tubes (15,000 cfs), for a combined magnitude up to about 45,000 cfs depending on the number of functional generators/penstocks, with release durations of about 2 to 7 days. Most HFEs are limited to a maximum duration of 96 hours under the 2011 HFE protocol, though some LTEMP alternatives allow extended-duration HFEs when adequate sediment supply is available.

Operation Rules
What limits and overriding constraints apply to extended-duration fall High-Flow Experiments (HFEs) under LTEMP Alternative D?
Under LTEMP Alternative D, extended-duration fall HFEs (greater than 96 hours) are capped at no more than four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period, triggered by the modeled sand mass balance from Paria River sediment inputs during the defined fall accounting period (July 1-November 30). However, an extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume -- meaning the legal requirement to meet the annual release volume can override an otherwise-triggered extended-duration fall HFE.

Operation Rules
What is Glen Canyon Dam's 'minimum power pool' elevation, and what current operational directive targets maintaining Lake Powell at or above it?
Glen Canyon Dam's design-basis minimum water surface elevation for power operation is 3,490 feet, with the eight penstock intakes centered at elevation 3,470 feet (about 45 feet above the estimated silt elevation projected after 150 years of reservoir operation). Reflecting this design threshold, Reclamation's March 2024 interim operating guidance directs exercising the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to attempt to maintain Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft, so as to preserve redundant downstream delivery through both the penstocks and the river outlet works.

Operation Rules
What river outlet works release capacity is available at Glen Canyon Dam as Lake Powell approaches low elevations, compared to full design capacity?
The river outlet works (four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes) were designed with an unrestricted capacity of 3,750 cfs per tube (15,000 cfs total) at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft (minimum power-operation water surface). Below elevation 3,550 ft, however, the 2024 LTEMP Final SEIS's modeling assumed a reduced capacity of 3,150 cfs per tube (12,600 cfs total) rather than the unrestricted 3,750 cfs/tube maximum. Separately, Reclamation's March 2024 interim operating guidance set even more granular, elevation-stepped interim maximum per-conduit flow limits to limit cavitation risk, including 3,185 cfs at elevation 3,490 ft, stepping down to 2,200 cfs at 3,420 ft, 1,200 cfs at 3,400 ft, and 0 cfs at 3,390 ft.

Operation Rules
What is the minimum objective annual release volume from Lake Powell established by the Long-Range Operating Criteria (LROC), and how is it referenced in subsequent operating documents?
The 1970 Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (LROC), Article II(2), establishes the objective of maintaining a minimum annual release from Lake Powell of 8.23 million acre-feet (maf). Reclamation returned to this objective minimum release beginning in 1988 after the 1980-1987 Long-Range Operating Criteria period. The 2007 Interim Guidelines, Section 6.C.1, likewise require a minimum of 8.23 maf to be released from Glen Canyon Dam each year, except for reductions specified by the Interim Guidelines. The 2008 Final Biological Opinion describes this 8.23 maf figure as Reclamation's baseline minimum objective annual release, with the proposed action allowing releases below it only under conditions defined in the Shortage Guidelines. As of the 2025 Post-2026 Alternatives Report, Reclamation affirms that under LROC Article II(2) the objective remains a minimum release of 8.23 maf, and plans to publish any annual deficits below that objective release alongside 10-year Lee Ferry aggregate flow metrics.

Operation Rules
What is the 2007 Interim Guidelines' Mid-Elevation Release Tier rule, and what release volume does it produce for Lake Powell in Water Year 2026?
Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines' Mid-Elevation Release Tier (Section 6.C), when the projected January 1 Lake Powell elevation is below 3,575 feet and at or above 3,525 feet, the Secretary releases 7.48 maf from Lake Powell in the Water Year if the projected January 1 Lake Mead elevation is at or above 1,025 feet (or 8.23 maf if Lake Mead is below 1,025 feet). Both the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan and the July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study confirm this Mid-Elevation Release Tier (per 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 6.C.1 and the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD Section 6.E) governs Lake Powell operations for Water Year 2026, with the August 2025 24-Month Study's most probable inflow scenario originally projecting a 7.48 maf release from Glen Canyon Dam for WY2026.

Operation Rules
What Lower Basin Shortage Condition applies when Lake Mead's January 1 elevation is projected between 1,050 and 1,075 feet, and how does it govern calendar year 2026 operations?
Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 2.D.1.a, when Lake Mead content is projected at or below elevation 1,075 feet and at or above 1,050 feet on January 1, a quantity of 7.167 maf is apportioned for Lower Division consumptive use, split 2.48 maf Arizona, 287,000 af Nevada, and 4.4 maf California -- described in CRS reporting as Reclamation curtailing Arizona and Nevada water deliveries below contracted levels once Lake Mead falls below elevation 1,075 feet (the first / Tier One level of shortage). The July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study confirms that, because the August 2025 24-Month Study projected the January 1, 2026 Lake Mead elevation below 1,075 feet and above 1,050 feet, a Section 2.D.1.a Shortage Condition -- together with Section III.B of Exhibit 1 to the Lower Basin Drought Contingency Plan Agreement -- governs Lake Mead operation for calendar year 2026.

Operation Rules
What is the four-tier elevation-based coordinated operations structure governing annual Lake Powell releases under the 2007 Interim Guidelines?
The Interim Guidelines for Coordinated Operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead define four operating tiers -- the Equalization Tier, Upper Elevation Balancing Tier, Mid-Elevation Release Tier, and Lower Elevation Balancing Tier -- with scheduled Lake Powell water-year releases adjusted each month based on forecast inflow and projected September 30 elevations at both reservoirs. In CRSS modeling of the Continued Current Strategies baseline, each January's governing tier is set by end-of-calendar-year pool elevation: the Equalization Tier applies at or above the Equalization Level; the Upper Elevation Balancing Tier applies down to elevation 3,575 feet; the Mid-Elevation Release Tier applies between 3,575 and 3,525 feet; and the Lower Elevation Balancing Tier applies below elevation 3,525 feet.

Operation Rules
What elevation condition triggers the Equalization Tier for Lake Powell releases, and what specific elevation threshold currently defines eligibility for equalization releases?
Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 6.A (Equalization Tier), if Lake Powell reaches the elevation stated in the Lake Powell Equalization Elevation Table for a given Water Year and the September 30 projected Lake Mead elevation is below 1,105 feet, the Secretary releases additional water from Lake Powell to Lake Mead until the reservoirs fully equalize, Lake Mead reaches 1,105 feet, or Lake Powell reaches 20 feet below its equalization elevation. Reclamation's 2004 interim 602(a) storage guideline, in effect through 2026, supplies the concrete current value implementing this mechanism: Lake Powell's elevation must be above 3,630 feet (approximately 14.85 maf of storage) for equalization releases between Lake Powell and Lake Mead to occur at all.

Operation Rules
Under the 2024 near-term operations agreement, what happens to Glen Canyon Dam releases if Lake Powell's elevation drops below 3,500 feet?
Under the 2024 near-term consensus agreement / 2024 ROD's new Section XI.G.6.E (per CRS summary and the official Record of Decision), if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 feet at Lake Powell in the next 12 months, the Secretary must begin planning to reduce Lake Powell releases as needed to not less than 6.0 maf for the Water Year to maintain elevation 3,500 feet -- in lieu of a 7.0 maf figure referenced under the near-term proposal framing.

Operation Rules
What Glen Canyon Dam release range applies when Lake Powell is at or below elevation 3,525 feet, under both the current 2007 Interim Guidelines and the proposed Post-2026 DEIS Basic Coordination Alternative?
Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines' Lower Elevation Balancing Tier (Section 6.D), when the projected January 1 Lake Powell elevation is below 3,525 feet, the Secretary balances the contents of Lake Mead and Lake Powell but releases not more than 9.5 maf and not less than 7.0 maf from Lake Powell in the Water Year. The Post-2026 Colorado River Reservoir Operations Draft EIS describes its Basic Coordination Alternative (the least-restrictive of four proposed post-2026 alternatives) as providing Glen Canyon Dam releases of 7.0 to 9.5 maf depending on Lake Powell elevation, with the lowest releases occurring at or below a Lake Powell elevation of 3,525 feet -- the same numeric range and elevation threshold as the current Lower Elevation Balancing Tier.

Operation Rules
What is Glen Canyon Dam's total powerplant/penstock discharge (release) capacity?
Sources disagree on Glen Canyon Dam's total powerplant/penstock discharge capacity. Two sources state approximately 31,500 cfs: a CRS report describes the dam's eight hydropower penstocks (elevation 3,470 ft, about 15 ft diameter each) as having 'a combined total discharge capacity of 31,500 cubic feet per second'; and a USGS historical data report states that before June 1990, fluctuating daily releases reached 'maxima at turbine capacity of 892 m3/s (31,500 cfs).' Two other sources state a higher figure of approximately 33,000-33,200 cfs: the LTEMP FEIS Chapter 1 states 'the powerplant can release a maximum of about 33,200 cfs of water' through 8 turbines; and a separate USGS report states the penstocks have 'a maximum release capacity of 934 m3/s (33,000 cfs).' The EUs do not explain this numeric discrepancy (e.g., whether it reflects design/nameplate capacity vs. an as-built or derated operational maximum, or different measurement conventions); both readings are preserved here rather than reconciled.

Operation Rules
What operating limits applied under Glen Canyon Dam's 1991 interim operating criteria (and the draft EIS preferred alternative), and how did the 1996 Record of Decision's final decision change them?
Beginning November 1, 1991, Reclamation implemented interim operating criteria for Glen Canyon Dam that cut the approved maximum peak release from 31,500 cfs to 20,000 cfs, restricted daily fluctuations to a range of 5,000-8,000 cfs, and capped ramp rates at 2,500 cfs/hour increasing and 1,500 cfs/hour decreasing, while still meeting the 8.23 maf minimum annual release. Between the draft and final EIS that led to the 1996 Record of Decision, these same starting values were revised: the up-ramp rate limit was increased from 2,500 to 4,000 cfs/hour, and the maximum allowable release was increased from 20,000 to 25,000 cfs, specifically to enhance power production flexibility in response to public comments.

Operation Rules
What operating alternative did Reclamation select for Glen Canyon Dam in the 1996 Record of Decision, and what did it replace?
In the 1996 Record of Decision, the Secretary selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) Alternative as Glen Canyon Dam's operating criteria, explicitly because it would reduce daily flow fluctuations well below the 'no action' (historic peaking) levels of releases while providing high steady releases of short duration to protect or enhance downstream resources, allowing limited flexibility for power operations. A peer-reviewed research paper confirms MLFF became the dam's operating regime in 1996, replacing hydroelectric peaking operations, and was the preferred alternative identified in the 1995 Environmental Impact Statement as an adaptive strategy for improving downstream Colorado River ecosystem resources.

Operation Rules
What is the release pattern of Trout Management Flows (TMFs) under LTEMP Alternative D, and what triggers their implementation?
Trout Management Flows (TMFs) under LTEMP Alternative D consist of repeated fluctuation cycles combining sustained high flows (e.g., 20,000 cfs, for 2 days to 1 week) with a rapid drop to a very low flow (e.g., 5,000-8,000 cfs), intended to strand young-of-year trout; up to three TMF cycles per month may be tested over as many as four months (May-August). Under the LTEMP preferred alternative, TMFs are triggered by the prediction of high recruitment of young-of-year rainbow trout at Lees Ferry, regardless of the cause of the trout population increase, with the specific implementation triggers developed each year in consultation with the Arizona Game and Fish Department (AZGFD) and other stakeholders based on that year's resource conditions.

Operation Rules
What defines a 'Normal Condition' (or 'Normal Water Supply Condition') for Lower Basin Colorado River deliveries under the current shortage-sharing framework?
Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 2.A, a 'Normal Condition' for Lake Mead exists in years when its January 1 elevation is projected to be above 1,075 feet and below 1,145 feet, in which case the Secretary determines either a Normal Condition or, per Section 2.B.5, an ICS Surplus Condition. The Post-2026 Colorado River Reservoir Operations Draft EIS (Chapter 1 background) restates this concept in outcome-based terms: a Normal Water Supply Condition exists when the Secretary determines that sufficient mainstream water is available to satisfy 7.5 maf of annual consumptive use in the Lower Division States.

Operation Rules
What is the Drought Response Operations Agreement (DROA) 'Target Elevation' at Lake Powell, and how is it used to prioritize drought response operations?
The Drought Response Operations Agreement (DROA) defines elevation 3,525 ft as the 'target elevation' at Lake Powell for minimizing the risk of the reservoir declining below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool), providing a 35-foot buffer above minimum power pool to allow response actions before Lake Powell drops below 3,490 ft. Under DROA, operational adjustments in monthly release volumes at Glen Canyon Dam are considered first to minimize the risk of Lake Powell declining below this Target Elevation, before releases from other CRSPA Initial Units (e.g., Flaming Gorge, Navajo, Aspinall) are evaluated as a subsequent response option.

Regulation / Governance
What did the 1922 Colorado River Compact apportion to the Upper and Lower Basins?
The Colorado River Compact of 1922 apportions the exclusive beneficial consumptive use of 7,500,000 acre-feet (7.5 MAF) of water per year, in perpetuity, to each of the Upper Basin and the Lower Basin (Compact Article III(a)). A CRS congressional report restates this same 7.5 MAF-per-basin apportionment and adds that the Lower Basin was also given the right to increase its beneficial consumptive use by an additional 1 MAF per year.

Regulation / Governance
What Colorado River operating instruments expire in 2026, and what post-2026 process do they trigger?
The 2007 Interim Guidelines were deliberately designed as a 20-year 'interim' framework and are scheduled to expire at the end of 2026, alongside other Colorado River operating instruments (the 2019 Drought Contingency Plans and international Minutes 323/330). This 2026 expiration is the trigger for Reclamation's post-2026 operations review: DOI formally initiated the Post-2026 NEPA process on June 16, 2023 to develop successor operating guidelines for Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam effective when the 2007 Interim Guidelines expire, and Basin States were subsequently asked to submit a preliminary post-2026 agreement by mid-November 2025 and a final seven-state agreement by mid-February 2026, targeting implementation for the 2027 operating year.

Operation Purposes
What purposes does the Colorado River Storage Project Act of 1956 authorize for Glen Canyon Dam?
The Colorado River Storage Project Act of 1956 authorizes Glen Canyon Dam for the purposes, among others, of: regulating the flow of the Colorado River; storing water for beneficial consumptive use; enabling the Upper Basin States to utilize their Colorado River Compact and Upper Colorado River Basin Compact apportionments; reclamation of arid lands; flood control; and generation of hydroelectric power, with hydropower generation explicitly framed as incident to the foregoing purposes.

Operation Purposes
What is the LTEMP's stated purpose and time frame?
The LTEMP's stated purpose is to provide a comprehensive framework for adaptively managing Glen Canyon Dam operations over a 20-year period, consistent with the Grand Canyon Protection Act (GCPA) and other applicable federal law. This purpose statement is repeated in near-identical language in both the 2016 LTEMP Record of Decision and the LTEMP Final EIS Chapter 1, and is independently corroborated by a 2021 Reclamation SECURE Water Act report to Congress describing LTEMP (finalized via EIS in October 2016) as establishing a 20-year adaptive management framework consistent with the GCPA.

Regulation / Governance
Does the LTEMP govern the total annual release volume from Glen Canyon Dam, or only the sub-annual release pattern?
The LTEMP (including its 2016 ROD and 2024 SEIS amendment) governs only the monthly, daily, and hourly release pattern from Glen Canyon Dam. It does not control the total annual release volume, which remains governed separately by the Long-Range Operating Criteria (LROC) as currently implemented through the 2007 Interim Guidelines (and, for the 2024 amendment, as further supplemented by the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS). Because of this scope boundary, LTEMP does not modify determinations made under the Interim Shortage Guidelines for Lake Powell and Lake Mead and does not trigger an off-cycle mid-year review of reservoir operations.

Regulation / Governance
What is the LROC's minimum annual release objective for Glen Canyon Dam, and what storage-balancing rule accompanies it?
Since 1970, the annual volume of water released from Glen Canyon Dam has been governed by the Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (LROC), which sets a minimum objective annual release of 8.23 million acre-feet and requires equalized storage between Lake Powell and Lake Mead. The Annual Operating Plan governs monthly operations and interagency agreements govern hourly operations within this framework; the 2007 Shortage ROD implements LROC provisions through 2026 and allows annual releases both above and below the 8.23 MAF minimum objective under specified conditions.

Regulation / Governance
What is the statutory basis and annual mechanism through which the 2007 Interim Guidelines are implemented?
The 2007 Interim Guidelines are implemented annually by the Secretary through the Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (LROC), established pursuant to the Colorado River Basin Project Act (CRBPA) of September 30, 1968, and issued via the Annual Operating Plan (AOP). The AOP itself is the single, integrated reference document required by Section 602(b) of the CRBPA of 1968, and it memorializes operational decisions made under multiple individual federal actions, including the Interim Surplus Guidelines, the 1996 Glen Canyon Dam ROD, and the 2007 Interim Guidelines.

Regulation / Governance
What is the Glen Canyon Dam Adaptive Management Program (GCDAMP) and what is its governance role relative to the Secretary of the Interior?
The Glen Canyon Dam Adaptive Management Program (GCDAMP/AMP) was established in 1997 (per its Record of Decision under the Grand Canyon Protection Act) as a federal advisory committee under FACA that evaluates dam operations and nonflow treatments' effects on Colorado River ecosystem resources, using monitoring and research results to make recommendations to DOI. Its formal structure comprises the Secretary's Designee, the Adaptive Management Work Group (AMWG), the Technical Work Group, the Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center, and Independent Review Panels, funded by Reclamation at approximately $8 million annually from power revenues. Critically, the Secretary of the Interior retains sole discretion to decide how best to accomplish dam operations and experiments in any given year; AMWG functions only in an advisory capacity.

Regulation / Governance
What role did structured/decision analysis play in selecting the LTEMP preferred alternative?
DOI deliberately uses the term 'decision analysis' (or 'structured decision analysis') rather than 'structured decision making' for the LTEMP EIS process, because the Secretary of the Interior retains sole statutory responsibility and authority to select the preferred alternative. Structured Decision Analysis (SDA) was incorporated into the LTEMP EIS as a voluntary stakeholder-input tool; it was not required by NEPA and was not the sole basis for selecting the preferred alternative. Instead, the preferred alternative was based on the full EIS analysis together with public comment, socioeconomic considerations, and AMWG stakeholder input, with SDA/decision-analysis outputs serving as an appendix to the Draft and Final EIS that informed, but did not replace, the Secretary's decision.

Regulation / Governance
What triggered the 2008 Biological Opinion on Glen Canyon Dam operations and what did it authorize?
Reclamation formally requested reinitiation of ESA Section 7 consultation on Glen Canyon Dam operations in a November 13, 2007 letter to FWS, based on new scientific information about listed-species status and dam-operation effects; FWS responded December 5, 2007 with the species list to be addressed (humpback chub, razorback sucker, Kanab ambersnail, southwestern willow flycatcher). This consultation produced the 2008 Final Biological Opinion, which replaced the 1995 Final BO on Glen Canyon Dam operations and authorized Reclamation's implementation of Modified Low Fluctuating Flows (MLFF) plus experimental dam operations for a five-year experimental period (remainder of WY2008 through 2012), after which Reclamation was expected to reconsult with FWS.

Operation Purposes
What is the generating capacity of the Glen Canyon powerplant?
An original ASCE engineering design paper describes the Glen Canyon Powerplant as designed for 900,000-kilowatt capacity, intended to generate the principal portion of electrical energy needed in the Upper Colorado River Basin, with surplus revenue used to help repay costs of Upper Basin participating projects authorized in 1956. Reclamation's current project page instead documents the powerplant's actual as-built configuration: eight turbines driving four 118,750-kilowatt and four 136,562-kilowatt generators, for a total nameplate generating capacity of 1,021,248 kilowatts. The two figures reflect different points in the project's history (original design estimate versus final as-built specification) rather than a direct contradiction.

Operation Purposes
What is Lake Powell's core operational role/purpose within the Colorado River system?
Lake Powell functions as the primary storage 'bank account' of the Colorado River Storage Project, holding approximately 80 percent of the total combined storage capacity of the four CRSP initial units; without this storage, annual water delivery obligations to the Lower Basin could likely not be met without creating significant shortages in the Upper Basin. More broadly, the reservoir serves multiple compatible operational purposes: hydroelectric power generation at Glen Canyon Dam, water storage banking for the Upper Colorado River Basin, stabilization of downstream water delivery commitments, and buffering the Lower Colorado River Basin (including Lake Mead) against sedimentation and hydrological fluctuations.

Regulation / Governance
What is the stated purpose of the 2007 Interim Guidelines?
The 2007 Interim Guidelines were developed to improve management of Colorado River water supplies and to provide water users a greater degree of predictability/certainty regarding the timing and volume of annual water deliveries and potential delivery reductions, particularly under drought and low-reservoir conditions.

Regulation / Governance
When were the interim operating criteria that became the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) regime established, and what did they set for Glen Canyon Dam releases?
Two sources describe the origin of the interim operating criteria that were later adopted as the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) regime via the 1996 Record of Decision, but they give different establishment dates. Reclamation's 2002 Report to Congress states the Secretary adopted interim operating criteria in November 1991 limiting Glen Canyon Dam minimum/maximum flows and daily fluctuations, later superseded by final operating criteria signed February 1997 (62 Fed. Reg. 9447) that cap releases at 25,000 cfs except during high inflow years or power system emergencies. A USGS historical data report instead states the 1996 ROD adopted, with slight modification, interim operating criteria established in August 1991 as the MLFF alternative. This date discrepancy (August vs. November 1991) is preserved here rather than resolved, since the underlying source excerpts do not clarify whether they refer to the same milestone (e.g., proposal versus formal Secretarial adoption).

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
What is Glen Canyon Dam's minimum power pool elevation, and what does it represent operationally?
Reclamation's original Technical Record of Design and Construction established elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum reservoir elevation for power production, 20 ft above the penstock intake centerline (elevation 3,470 ft); water cannot be released through the penstocks below 3,490 ft (OFF-025-03). Multiple later sources restate this same threshold: Reclamation estimates the depth for minimum power pool is 20 ft above the penstocks, i.e. elevation 3,490 fasl (CRS-002-02); at 3,490 ft, minimum power pool is 20 ft above the generators' actual penstock intakes, and the dam's eight turbines must be shut down at minimum power pool to avoid cavitation (MED-002-01); the 1999 multi-level intake structure hydraulic model study likewise designates elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum water surface for power operations (OFF-028-06); the 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states hydropower production would cease if Lake Powell drops below approximately 3,490 ft (OFF-005-01); the 2024 Near-term Operations SEIS ROD notes dry hydrology in recent years produced low Lake Powell elevations at levels such as 3,490 ft, giving Reclamation operating experience at this threshold (OFF-002-06); the 2024 LTEMP Final Supplemental EIS states Reclamation's Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels directs use of the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to try to keep Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft (OFF-007-03); and an April 2026 status report reiterates that hydropower generation stops at 3,490 feet, with the reservoir at 3,526 feet at that time and Reclamation aiming to keep it above 3,500 feet (MED-001-04).

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
What is Lake Powell's maximum live (usable) storage capacity at elevation 3,700 ft?
Reclamation's Upper Colorado Region CRSP Glen Canyon Unit Quick Facts page states Lake Powell's live capacity at elevation 3,700 feet is 24,322,000 acre-feet (OFF-029-01). The 2016 LTEMP Final EIS Chapter 3 similarly states Lake Powell has a maximum live storage capacity of about 24.3 maf (OFF-005-01), matching the Quick Facts figure.

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
What is Lake Powell's total storage capacity at full pool (elevation 3,700 ft), per pre-2018-resurvey estimates?
The 2016 LTEMP Final EIS Chapter 1 states Lake Powell has more than 26 million acre-feet of water storage capacity (OFF-004-10). The 2002 Report to Congress states Lake Powell holds approximately 26.2 million acre-feet of Colorado River water (OFF-009-02). USGS's 1964-2013 historical data series, citing Ferrari (1988), states that at full pool elevation 3,700 ft Lake Powell has a capacity of 26.214 maf (RES-019-01). These three sources, spanning 1988 through 2016, are mutually consistent at approximately 26.2 maf.

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
What is Lake Powell's current total (and active) storage capacity at full pool, per the most recent (2018) USGS resurvey?
The 2017-18 USGS topobathymetric survey determined Lake Powell's storage capacity at full pool (elevation 3,702.91 ft NAVD88) to be 25,160,000 acre-feet, a 6.79 percent decrease from the 1963 pre-impoundment estimate (RES-013-01). The USBR project database (Project ID 144) reports a matching figure: total capacity for Lake Powell is 25.16 million acre-feet, of which 23.4 million acre-feet is active capacity (OFF-030-01).

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
How much has Lake Powell's storage capacity declined since 1963, per the 2018 USGS topobathymetric resurvey?
The 2018 USGS resurvey documents multiple, complementary measures of capacity loss since the reservoir's 1963 pre-impoundment baseline: (1) full-pool (elevation 3,702.91 ft NAVD88) storage capacity decreased 6.79 percent (1,833,000 acre-feet), from the 1963 estimate to 25,160,000 acre-feet in 2018 (RES-013-01); (2) areal extent at full pool decreased 1.33 percent from 1963 to 2018 (and 0.96 percent from 1986 to 2018), reaching 159,200 acres in spring 2018 (RES-013-02); (3) dead storage capacity (below elevation 3,372.91 ft NAVD88, below all penstocks and outlet works) decreased 8.11 percent (152,900 acre-feet) from 1963 to 2018, and inactive storage (up to elevation 3,492.91 ft NAVD88, the lowest elevation at which all penstocks are submerged) decreased 9.84 percent (599,900 acre-feet) over the same period (RES-013-04).

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
What is Lake Powell's active/usable storage capacity, as distinguished from its total (gross) capacity?
The CRSS model documentation for the Post-2026 DEIS states the assumed maximum storage for Lake Powell used in CRSS modeling is 23,314,000 acre-feet (Table A-2) (OFF-021-05). The USBR project database separately reports Lake Powell's active capacity as 23.4 million acre-feet, distinct from its 25.16 maf total capacity (OFF-030-01).

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
What is the elevation of Glen Canyon Dam's river outlet works, and what does it represent for Lake Powell's operating range?
The 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states Glen Canyon Dam is designed to operate between the outlet works intake elevation of 3,370 ft AMSL and the top of the live storage pool at 3,700 ft AMSL (OFF-005-01). High Country News reporting states that if Lake Powell drops to the river outlet works' (ROW) elevation of 3,370 feet, the reservoir reaches "dead pool," where water passes through the dam only when river flow exceeds evaporation losses, with no lower intakes or spillways available (MED-002-04). The 2018 USGS resurvey, using the NAVD88 vertical datum, places the dead storage elevation (below all hydroelectric penstocks and other outlet works) at 3,372.91 ft NAVD88 (RES-013-04).

Storage Capacity and Storage Targets
How are Lake Powell's scheduled water-year releases adjusted when operations are in the equalization tier, upper elevation balancing tier, or lower elevation balancing tier?
The 2007 Biological Assessment on Experimental Releases from Glen Canyon Dam states that when Lake Powell and Lake Mead operations are in the equalization tier, upper elevation balancing tier, or lower elevation balancing tier under the 2007 Shortage ROD, scheduled Lake Powell water-year releases are adjusted each month based on forecasted inflow and projected September 30 active storage at both Lake Powell and Lake Mead (OFF-011-05). The 2008 Final Biological Opinion for Glen Canyon Dam operations restates the same rule in nearly identical language, per the Shortage Guidelines ROD, and additionally notes that releases greater than 9.5 maf generally occur during equalization of storage contents between the two reservoirs (OFF-012-05).

Inflow Forecast
What was the official Water Year 2026 unregulated inflow forecast for Lake Powell as of July 2026?
The July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study reports the full WY2026 unregulated inflow forecast for Lake Powell as 3.50 maf, 36 percent of the 1991-2020 average (OFF-023-05). The Lower Colorado Weekly Hydrologic Update dated July 27, 2026 reports the WY2026 unregulated inflow forecast as 3,501 kaf (36% of normal), an increase of 10 kaf from the previous forecast of 3,491 kaf (also 36% of normal) (OFF-024-02).

Inflow Forecast
How does Water Year 2026 inflow into Lake Powell compare to the historical record, and what is driving the record or near-record low?
Circle of Blue reporting (April 2026) states inflows into Lake Powell in 2026 are projected to be the lowest ever measured, breaking the previous record set in 2002, driven by a downward snowpack trend and a March 2026 heat wave that was the most extreme on record in the Southwest for that time of year (MED-001-05). Reclamation's newsroom release states Lake Powell's water year 2026 minimum probable inflow is forecasted at just 2.78 million acre-feet, 29 percent of historical average and one of the lowest on record, with Reclamation's April 24-Month Study projecting Lake Powell may decline below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool) by August 2026 without major intervention (OFF-035-01).

Operation Failure
What operational constraint does Glen Canyon Dam face when Lake Powell falls below the minimum power pool elevation of 3,490 feet, and what release-capacity shortfall results?
When Lake Powell drops below the minimum power pool elevation of 3,490 feet, Glen Canyon Dam can no longer release water through its powerplant turbines/penstocks and must rely on the river outlet works (ROW), whose capacity is limited and increases with pool elevation (OFF-021-08); the Post-2026 Draft EIS states the dam 'was not envisioned to operate below minimum power pool (elevation 3,490 feet)' and that below this elevation water must be released through the jet tubes at the end of the ROW instead of the penstocks (OFF-019-05). Across all anticipated post-2026 operating alternatives, releases from Lake Powell may fall below the alternative's specified release volume at elevations below 3,490 feet due to this infrastructure limitation (OFF-020-04). A separate study quantified the resulting shortfall: at elevation 3,430 feet, the ROW can discharge only 10,200 cfs (7.41 MAF/year), considerably less than the Law of the River's 8.23 MAF/year delivery requirement, and below the ROW's own elevation of 3,370 feet, approximately 1.89 MAF becomes inaccessible dead storage (CRS-002-08).

Uncertainty and Risk Management
Can the river outlet works (ROW) reliably serve as the sole long-term release mechanism for Glen Canyon Dam at low Lake Powell reservoir levels?
Multiple sources indicate the river outlet works (ROW) were not designed for, and cannot be fully relied upon for, long-term or high-flow releases at low Lake Powell levels. Reclamation's 2024 Technical Decision Memorandum found no design reference indicating the ROW were intended for long-term water conveyance at low reservoir levels; historically they were used only to augment powerplant/spillway discharges for short durations (e.g., about three months during 1983 flood releases, days to a week for high-flow experiments) (OFF-025-04). A 2023 special inspection found the hollow-jet valves, pipes, and ring-follower gates sufficient for periodic/seasonal releases but flagged concern about long-term high-flow use and recommended a major overhaul or replacement for high confidence in continuous long-term operation (OFF-025-05). This concern has historical precedent: on April 20, 1965, at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft with the ROW variably open, the dam's tailrace stabilization slab was undermined by a recirculating eddy from ROW operation and portions of it collapsed, because tailwater was 4-6 feet lower than had been predicted by physical modeling (OFF-025-06). More recently, in 2023, when the ROW were used for a high-flow release into the Grand Canyon at low-reservoir levels, damaging cavitation occurred, and the Bureau has warned further extended use would likely cause more (MED-002-03). Based on this evidence, Reclamation's formal conclusion is that it should not rely on the ROW as the sole means of releasing water from Glen Canyon Dam, as would be required below minimum power pool (3,490 ft), given current uncertainty about long-term conduit and hollow-jet valve performance and tailrace sedimentation (OFF-025-07).

Uncertainty and Risk Management
How severe was the 2000-2022 Colorado River Basin drought period relative to the historical and paleoclimate record, as cited in recent operating decisions?
Two independent Reclamation documents state the identical drought-severity statistic: the period from 2000 through 2022 was the driest/lowest 23-year period in more than a century of record and one of the driest/lowest such periods in the last 1,200 years in the Colorado River Basin. The 2024 Near-term Colorado River Operations SEIS Record of Decision cites this as the basis for supplementing the 2007 Interim Guidelines (OFF-002-07), and the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan restates the same statistic while separately reporting that total system storage fell by 3.37 MAF during water year 2025, from 43 percent to 37 percent of capacity (OFF-022-07).

Uncertainty and Risk Management
What did the 2012 Colorado River Basin Water Supply and Demand Study find regarding future basin-wide water supply-demand shortfalls?
The Colorado River Basin Water Supply and Demand Study (2012) found that future water supply and demand imbalances in the Colorado River Basin could produce shortfalls of 2.3 to 4.1 MAF per year during deficit periods, rising to approximately 7.4 MAF per year during deficit periods once climate change effects are factored in (OFF-005-18, citing Reclamation 2012e). Reclamation's own program summary of that same Study confirms this conclusion in qualitative terms, stating the Study "confirmed...there are likely to be significant shortfalls between projected water supplies and demands in the Colorado River Basin in the coming decades" (OFF-016-02).

Uncertainty and Risk Management
What significance does the Lake Mead elevation of 1,000 feet hold as a basin-wide risk/vulnerability threshold in Colorado River operations?
A Lake Mead elevation of 1,000 feet functions as a recurring basin-wide risk/vulnerability threshold in Colorado River risk management. The 2007 Interim Guidelines ROD establishes a mandatory annual consultation requirement: whenever Lake Mead is below elevation 1,025 feet, the Secretary must consult with the Basin States on whether hydrologic conditions and anticipated deliveries are likely to cause Lake Mead to fall below 1,000 feet, and must implement any additional measures consistent with applicable federal law (OFF-001-09). Separately, the 2016 SECURE Water Act report describes the Colorado River Basin Water Supply and Demand Study's use of Lake Mead elevation dropping below 1,000 feet in any month as one of two defined system-reliability vulnerability metrics (the other being a 'Lee Ferry deficit,' when the 10-year running total flow at Lee Ferry falls below 75 MAF) (OFF-018-04).

Operation Failure
What take-exceedance thresholds did FWS establish to define failure of the March 2008 Glen Canyon Dam high flow test relative to protected species?
The Final Biological Opinion for the Operation of Glen Canyon Dam (2008) set two species-specific surrogate take-exceedance thresholds for the March 2008 high flow test, beyond which FWS would consider anticipated take exceeded and trigger a required review of reasonable and prudent measures: (1) for humpback chub, more than 20 mortalities attributable to the high flow test (OFF-012-11); and (2) for Kanab ambersnail, more than 117 m2 (1,259 ft2) of habitat removed at Vaseys Paradise and attributable to the high flow test (OFF-012-12).

Operation Failure
What economic and operational impact did the 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) restrictions have on Glen Canyon Dam hydropower operations?
The 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) operating criteria reduced Glen Canyon Dam powerplant's operating flexibility and, consequently, its economic value. An ex post economic analysis found this reduction in flexibility prompted the Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) to modify commitments made to its customers (RES-026-01). A separate LTEMP EIS accounting found that between 1997 and 2005, this operational restriction cost WAPA and its power customers an average of $38 million to $50 million per year, since MLFF ramping restrictions prevented generation from adjusting hourly to match power demand, forcing increased reliance on alternate generating resources (OFF-005-08).

Uncertainty and Risk Management
What risk does warmer Glen Canyon Dam releases, caused by reduced Lake Powell storage, pose to humpback chub via nonnative-fish predation and competition?
Reduced Lake Powell storage, by warming Glen Canyon Dam releases, has been identified as a risk pathway for increased nonnative-fish predation and competition pressure on humpback chub. River warming that occurred from 2003 to 2011 (and again in 2014), resulting from reduced Lake Powell storage, was intended to benefit native humpback chub, but the Grand Canyon Ecosystem Model predicted that nonnative fish would also benefit, potentially increasing predation/competition risk to humpback chub through greater fish interactions in critical river segments (RES-014-06). Consistent with this risk pathway, the 2008 Final Biological Opinion notes that because prolonged droughts (paleoclimate tree-ring records show droughts of 15-20 years) could lower Lake Powell storage and raise dam release temperatures, increasing nonnative predation risk to humpback chub, Reclamation committed to monitor and control nonnative fish as necessary through the Adaptive Management Program if such warming occurs (OFF-012-18).

Uncertainty and Risk Management
How sensitive was the LTEMP preferred long-term operating strategy to the critical scientific/system uncertainties evaluated in the supporting decision analysis?
A decision analysis supporting LTEMP development found that the ranking of preferred long-term operating strategies was not sensitive to the critical scientific/system uncertainties evaluated (trout-humpback chub dynamics, trout-management-flow effectiveness, HFE effects on trout), but was sensitive mainly to stakeholders' value-based weighting of resource goals, with long-term hydrological input pattern being the one uncertainty that slightly affected rankings (RES-024-02). This was assessed using the expected value of perfect information (EVPI), which sets an upper bound on the value of experimental or adaptive management by comparing expected performance under uncertainty to expected performance if uncertainty could be fully resolved before a decision, and the related expected value of partial information (EVXI), which evaluates the value of resolving only part of the uncertainty (RES-024-07). The quantitative result: EVPI for the critical scientific uncertainties (fall HFE effect on trout, trout-management-flow effectiveness, temperature-versus-trout effect on humpback chub) was essentially zero for nearly all stakeholder weightings -- the same best-performing long-term strategy was identified across all 16 combinations of competing hypotheses for 12 of 14 stakeholders, and the two exceptions had an EVPI of less than 0.1 percent (RES-024-17).

Operation Failure
What operational failure occurred with dissolved oxygen in Glen Canyon Dam releases in September 2005, and what caused it?
In fall 2005, a plume of oxygen-depleted water in Lake Powell was captured in the penstock withdrawal zone and exported through Glen Canyon Dam, dropping tailwater dissolved oxygen below 4.0 mg/L in September 2005 and violating EPA cold-water fishery DO criteria (1-day mean minimum 4.0 mg/L, 7-day mean minimum 5.0 mg/L, 30-day mean 6.5 mg/L) (RES-020-02). This occurred because in most years the metalimnetic oxygen minimum sits well above the penstock elevation (3,470 ft) and does not affect dam discharges, but in 2005 reservoir elevations were the lowest since initial filling, placing the low-DO metalimnetic layer just above the penstock elevation and allowing oxygen-depleted water to pass through the dam (RES-020-07).

Operation Failure
What early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives, and why?
Two early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments, predating the LTEMP HFE protocol, failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives, each for a different reason. The November 3, 1997 Test Flow (a constant 872 m3/s release for 48 hours), Reclamation's first attempt at a post-tributary-flood sediment-redistribution release, did not significantly aggrade sandbars because its magnitude was insufficient to distribute sand to open depositional locations at higher elevations (RES-018-09). The 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment (a 4-day 864 m3/s release, 3 months of constant 227 m3/s, then a 4-day 881 m3/s release) produced minimal sandbar building because the Paria River had supplied very little sediment beforehand, and the sustained low, steady discharge instead allowed proliferation of invasive tamarisk seedlings on bare sand deposits (RES-018-10).

Operation Failure
What has been the long-term effectiveness of the High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol at rebuilding different types of Grand Canyon sandbars?
The long-term effectiveness of the High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol at rebuilding Grand Canyon sandbars differs by bar type and has structural limits at both ends. At wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits, vegetation stabilization and vertical aggradation during successive HFEs have progressively narrowed the channel and reduced the accommodation space available for further deposition, so at best HFEs can only replace sediment eroded during normal dam operations between events rather than produce net growth (RES-018-12). At separation bars and undifferentiated eddy bars, HFEs have not effectively rebuilt the bars, which have continued to gradually decrease in volume over time; although these bars consistently aggrade during individual HFEs, the subsequent erosion at these unvegetated, wind-exposed sites is rapid (RES-018-13).

A near-record-low WY2026 inflow forecast was classified through the CRSS/24-Month Study process into the Mid-Elevation Release Tier band, which triggered the 2024 SEIS ROD's Section 6.E emergency-reduction authority once the minimum-probable study projected Lake Powell below 3,500 ft; Interior then set the WY2026 release at 6.00 maf (down from the tier's default 7.48 maf) and paired it with a DROA-triggered supplemental release from Flaming Gorge Reservoir, publicly announced through Reclamation's April 2026 newsroom release.
A retrieval system answering 'why is the 2026 Glen Canyon release only 6.0 maf instead of 7.48 maf' should surface the full forecast-to-implementation chain (inflow forecast, tier classification, Section 6.E override, quantified release and Flaming Gorge package, public announcement), not just the final release figure.
