decision_process
Since 2012, Paria River tributary sand inputs are tracked and used to run a fall sand-mass-balance accounting process (July 1-November 30) that determines HFE eligibility; the formal 2012 protocol and 2016 LTEMP ROD translate that sediment signal into a release of up to ~45,000 cfs combining full powerplant and bypass-tube capacity, but the same ROD lets the legal requirement to meet the annual release volume override an otherwise-eligible extended-duration HFE, and post-release monitoring feeds back into the program's understanding of protocol effectiveness.
A user asking why a longer HFE was not run in a given year needs to see both the sediment-trigger logic and the annual-volume override, since either one alone could explain a non-implemented extended HFE.

constraint_structure
Below elevation 3,490 ft, Glen Canyon Dam's release path narrows from eight penstocks to only the river outlet works (ROW), whose own per-tube capacity is further reduced by cavitation limits as elevation falls; Reclamation's own 2024 assessment additionally concludes the ROW cannot be reliably used as a sole long-term release path, while the Law of the River's 8.23 maf/year minimum objective release remains legally in force regardless of this shrinking physical capacity -- together defining why Reclamation treats 3,490 ft (and the 3,525 ft DROA buffer above it) as hard operating priorities rather than discretionary targets.
This constraint structure is the physical basis for the emergency drought-response actions analyzed in SC-LP-001 and SC-LP-009; a report or index should link the physical-capacity constraint directly to those decision/regime-change cards rather than presenting them independently.
source_locators: OFF-025 (2024 Technical Decision Memorandum), Sections D.2, D.4, D.5, and E; MED-002 (High Country News), main article body.

index_text:
constraint_structure
The 1996 ROD set a baseline safety/recreation-driven envelope (minimum/maximum release, ramp rates, and a 3-tier daily-fluctuation cap) grounded in a 1995 river-guide/public preference study; the 2016 LTEMP ROD then revised the fluctuation formula and down-ramp rate specifically to reduce sandbar erosion, while WAPA continues to exercise discretionary hourly/weekly dispatch choices inside these limits that it can alter without a new NEPA/ROD process, leaving the up-ramp rate the one figure unchanged since 1996.
Distinguishes 'hard' ROD-level limits that require a NEPA/ROD process to change from WAPA's day-to-day discretionary dispatch choices that can shift without formal process -- relevant to any question about whether Glen Canyon Dam could operate differently tomorrow versus only after rulemaking.

operational_tradeoff
The 1996 ROD selected MLFF specifically to reduce daily flow fluctuations well below historic peaking levels in order to protect downstream sediment, fish, and recreation resources; this benefit to the ecosystem objective came at a documented, quantified cost to the power objective, reducing WAPA's operating flexibility and costing WAPA and its customers an average of $38-50 million per year between 1997 and 2005, while the LTEMP framework's Grand Canyon Protection Act mandate leaves total annual release volume (and the bulk of associated hydropower revenue) outside its scope.
Any economic argument for loosening MLFF/LTEMP constraints further should be benchmarked against this same historical $38-50 million/year estimate, and any environmental argument for tightening them should note that the annual-volume/hydropower-revenue base itself is legally untouched by LTEMP.
source_locators: OFF-005 (2016 LTEMP Final EIS), Section 3.13.1.4 Scheduling; RES-026 (ex post power economic analysis), abstract.

index_text:
operational_tradeoff
Extended-duration fall HFEs are designed to maximize sediment redistribution when tributary sand supply is high, but the 2016 LTEMP ROD explicitly subordinates this ecological opportunity to the legal annual-release-volume obligation: an eligible extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if doing so would affect that year's annual release volume, meaning the delivery obligation automatically wins whenever the two objectives conflict.
Report language explaining why an extended HFE did not occur in a given year must check both the sediment trigger and this volume-protection override before concluding sediment supply alone was insufficient.

operational_tradeoff
Reduced Lake Powell storage during drought warms Glen Canyon Dam releases in a way intended to benefit native humpback chub, but the same warming is modeled to also benefit nonnative fish, raising predation and competition pressure on humpback chub; Reclamation has responded with targeted suppression and management flows (2003-2005 fluctuating suppression releases, and Trout Management Flows under LTEMP Alternative D) and has institutionally committed to monitor and control nonnative fish if drought-driven warming recurs.
A low-storage/warm-release period should be flagged in monitoring and reporting as a compound risk period requiring both temperature and nonnative-fish-suppression tracking, not a temperature check alone.

operating_regime_change
Glen Canyon Dam moved from an unrestricted hydroelectric peaking regime to a tightly restricted 1991 interim-criteria regime, and then to the 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow regime, which restored some of the power flexibility cut in 1991 (raising the up-ramp rate and maximum release) while still holding fluctuations well below historic peaking levels, explicitly to protect downstream resources.
Distinguishes three sequential and legally distinct regimes (peaking / 1991 interim / 1996 MLFF) that a knowledge base should not conflate when answering historical questions about what rules applied in a given year.

operating_regime_change
The 2000-2022 period, the driest 23-year stretch in over a century of record, drove system storage down and produced a near-record-low WY2026 inflow forecast; this sustained drought prompted new, elevation-triggered emergency authorities (the 2024 near-term agreement's Section 6.E release-reduction authority and the 2024 interim ROW operating guidance) that in 2026 were actually invoked to cut the Glen Canyon release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf and pair it with a DROA-triggered Flaming Gorge release -- an emergency regime that supplements, rather than replaces, the standing MLFF/Interim Guidelines framework.
Shows the current emergency regime is additive and triggered, not a wholesale replacement of MLFF/Interim Guidelines; a report or index should present 2026 operations as 'baseline framework plus active emergency trigger,' not as a new standalone regime.
source_locators: OFF-023 (July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study), opening operations narrative, p.1; OFF-035 (Reclamation newsroom release), news release body.

index_text:
operating_regime_change
The 2007 Interim Guidelines were deliberately designed as a 20-year interim framework set to expire at the end of 2026, and this scheduled expiration formally triggered DOI's Post-2026 NEPA process in 2023; Basin States face a mid-February 2026 deadline for a final seven-state agreement targeting 2027 implementation, and at least one proposed post-2026 alternative (the Basic Coordination Alternative) is designed to continue the current Lower Elevation Balancing Tier's numeric range rather than replace it outright.
Any 2027-onward operational forecasting should track the seven-state agreement's February 2026 deadline as the real go/no-go milestone, since a failure to reach agreement would leave the specific post-2026 operating rule undetermined even though the current guidelines formally expire regardless.

historical_operation_failure
In September 2005, Glen Canyon Dam tailwater dissolved oxygen fell below EPA cold-water-fishery criteria because historically low reservoir elevations placed the reservoir's low-oxygen metalimnetic layer directly at the penstock withdrawal elevation, allowing oxygen-depleted water to be exported through the dam -- a documented water-quality failure mode tied specifically to low reservoir elevation.
Reinforces that minimum-power-pool-adjacent elevations create a water-quality risk pathway in addition to the well-documented power/release-capacity risk pathway analyzed in SC-LP-003; worth tracking as a distinct monitoring trigger at low elevations.

historical_operation_failure
On April 20, 1965, the Glen Canyon Dam river outlet works tailrace stabilization slab was partially undermined and collapsed because actual tailwater elevation ran 4-6 feet lower than the physical hydraulic model had predicted; Reclamation's 2024 Technical Decision Memorandum cites this 60-year-old event, together with 2023 inspection findings and 2023 cavitation damage, as direct historical evidence supporting its formal conclusion that the ROW should not be relied upon as Glen Canyon Dam's sole long-term release mechanism.
This 60-year-old precedent is being actively used today as load-bearing evidence in current (2024) infrastructure-risk decisions about low-elevation operations; a report on ROW reliability should present it as directly relevant history, not a closed historical footnote.

historical_operation_failure
Two early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments predating the current HFE protocol -- the November 1997 Test Flow and the 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment -- failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives for two different documented reasons (insufficient release magnitude versus insufficient antecedent sediment supply), a pattern of failure consistent with the post-2012 protocol's redesign to explicitly time releases to tributary sand inputs rather than a fixed schedule.
Supports treating sediment-supply timing as the single most important design variable for HFE effectiveness, ahead of release magnitude alone.

operational_consequence
Reclamation projects that its combined 2026 drought-response package -- reducing the WY2026 Glen Canyon release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf and releasing 660,000 acre-feet to 1 maf from Flaming Gorge Reservoir into Lake Powell by April 2027 -- will raise Lake Powell's elevation by about 54 feet, to at least 3,500 feet, by April 2027, starting from an April 2026 minimum-probable forecast that had projected a possible decline below the 3,490 ft minimum power pool by August 2026 absent intervention.
This card should be revisited once later 2026-2027 24-Month Studies are available, to convert it from a projected to an observed consequence, and to check the Flaming Gorge release volume actually delivered against the 660,000 AF-1 maf commitment.
source_locators: OFF-035 (Reclamation newsroom release), news release body; OFF-023 (July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study), opening operations narrative, p.1.

index_text:
operational_consequence
The 45-site long-term sandbar monitoring network shows the HFE protocol produced measurable short-term sandbar growth immediately following the 2012-2014 HFEs, but its long-term consequence diverges structurally by bar type: wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits can now at best only replace sediment eroded between events due to vegetation-driven channel narrowing, while separation and undifferentiated eddy bars have not been durably rebuilt at all because rapid erosion at these unvegetated, wind-exposed sites outpaces each HFE's gains.
A report claiming HFEs do or do not 'work' should specify which of the two structurally different bar types it means, since the observed consequence is genuinely bifurcated rather than uniform across the monitored sandbar population.
